#6566. Students Test Prototype Landing Pad to Make Lunar Operations Safe

When spacecraft perform vertical landing and takeoff maneuvers from the lunar surface, the results are very messy! Beyond the intense heat produced by the rocket engines, the force also kicks up regolith, the particulate dust that covers most of the lunar surface. With so many crewed and cargo missions planned for the coming years, space agencies are contracting with commercial partners to develop infrastructure that will keep spacecraft, astronauts, and other surface elements safe from all "moondust."

This includes landing pads that provide a stable surface and barrier for vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) vehicles. To help them realize their objectives under the Artemis Program, NASA has enlisted engineers from the University of Alabama in Huntsville (UAH) to create some. Their work is part of a multi-year partnership with Linc Research Inc., a certified engineering company located in Huntsville, Alabama, and supported through NASA's Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) program.

The student research team is led by Dr. Judy Schneider, a professor in UAH's Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering. Their research is focused on developing a design for modular, vented landing pads that will allow for safe transits to and from the lunar surface. This summer, the team successfully conducted three rocket-motor firing tests on a prototype of their landing pad at the university's Propulsion Research Center, demonstrating its ability to capture and redirect rocket exhaust through an integrated vent system.

Rocket-motor firing tests on a prototype lunar landing pad at the UAH Propulsion Research Center. Credit: Cadis Ammons

On Earth, landing pads consist of a solid structure capable of withstanding the full force and heat of a rocket plume. This can result in significant damage to the pad itself, as demonstrated by the first launch attempt of SpaceX's Starship prototype, including cratering beneath the mounting structure and sending debris flying in all directions. In contrast, the UAH team's design uses interlocking components with channels that help reduce thermal damage and protect the structure as well as the spacecraft.

For the tests, the team created individual concrete components and arranged them into a prototype measuring 3.65 m (12 ft) in diameter. The concrete serves as an analog for building materials that could be produced from lunar regolith, either "sintered" to form 3D-printed ceramics or combined with a bonding agent to produce "lunacrete." The components also had integrated sensors to record how the rocket plume's exhaust was channeled through the vent systems during the three firings.

The modular design also makes it easier to build on the Moon, where manufacturing centers are likely to be space-constrained. Smaller, individual components also mean future landing pads will be easier to assemble, expand, maintain, and repair over time. Combined with the use of local resources for building materials - aka. In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) - the team's goal could help make large-scale lunar infrastructure more feasible.

Earth's fluffy, dense atmosphere also helps prevent rocket exhaust plumes from expanding freely and kicking up dust. Because its only natural satellite is an airless body, dust clouds caused by impacts or rockets can travel all the way to the other side of the Moon. As a result, powerful blasts during takeoff and landing can propel dust at high speeds, potentially damaging nearby habitats, power elements, equipment, and other infrastructure. The dust can also be thrown into orbit, where it could interfere with orbiting satellites, space stations, and incoming spacecraft.

This marks a major step in developing landing infrastructure that will enable a lunar base and crewed operations in the near future. As Schneider said in a UHA press release:

On Earth, we use water-cooled flame buckets to redirect rocket exhaust. But we won't have those resources on the lunar surface, where water will be in limited supply. Our goal is to redirect the rocket plume so it doesn't damage the landing vehicle or any surrounding structures. The hot-fire tests demonstrated that we could redirect the rocket plume. By using an internally vented structure, we were able to prevent the heat from damaging the pad as it could in a solid structure.

With the initial tests complete, the team is now working on a 6 m-diameter (20 ft) landing pad that will be delivered to NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center (also in Huntsville) for additional testing and evaluation. These tests will further assess the design, push its technological readiness, and determine if the vented, modular approach can be scaled and adapted for repeated use. These efforts will bring the technology another step towards realization and deployment on the Moon.

Further Reading: University of Alabama Huntsville

Matt Williams is a space journalist, science communicator, and author with several published titles and studies. #6565. 53 Healthy Thanksgiving Recipes to Brighten Up the Table

What makes a healthy Thanksgiving recipe? To us, it’s less about cutting out butter or skipping pie and more about bringing balance to the table. Crisp, bitter greens make creamy mashed potatoes taste even better. Tart cranberries cut through rich turkey gravy. Beans, whole grains, and plenty of colorful vegetables bring flavor, texture, and variety to a meal that can otherwise skew decidedly beige.

These healthy Thanksgiving recipes cover the entire feast, from crunchy salads and make-ahead appetizers to satisfying plant-forward mains and festive desserts. Some offer more fiber or protein; others give seasonal produce a starring role. What they have in common is that every one is delicious. You’ll also find plenty of vegan, gluten-free, and dairy-free options too. Because there’s room for everyone—and everything—at the Thanksgiving table.

Deep purple cabbage, bitter radicchio, juicy citrus, and ruby-red pomegranate seeds make a strong case for putting salad front and center. Give the cabbage a good massage to soften it without sacrificing its crunch.

“In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake,” writes Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser. Here, thinly sliced pears get a shower of honey-roasted seeds and shaved cheese.

Instead of tender greens that might wilt before everyone sits down, consider a fennel salad that stays crunchy for hours. Walnuts, Parmesan, croutons, and lemon give it plenty of flavor and texture.

Who says salad has to be cold? Caramelized cauliflower, warm feta, crunchy pistachios, and sticky dates meet peppery arugula and a tangy vinaigrette. Hearty enough to satisfy, with plenty of greens to keep things fresh.

Bitter radicchio meets sweet apple and mustardy croutons in this hearty autumn salad. Tossing the apple slices with cider vinegar helps keep them from browning before the feast begins.

A Thanksgiving salad should be sturdy enough to hold its own on the buffet table. This one only gets better after it’s dressed, as the kale softens and the nutty pecan vinaigrette works its way into the leaves.

Cranberry sauce isn’t just for turkey. A tart dressing made with the canned stuff brings holiday spirit to bitter greens, sweetened pecans, and Manchego cheese. Consider it a little insurance against salad fatigue.

Warm spices and sweet carrots give this hearty lentil salad plenty of character. The legumes add plant-based protein and fiber, making it a substantial addition to a vegetarian Thanksgiving spread.

Panzanella isn’t just for summer. Swap ripe tomatoes for juicy oranges, add bitter chicories and shaved fennel, and toss everything with toasted pumpernickel croutons and a balsamic-Dijon vinaigrette.

Roasted carrots, chickpeas, almonds, and smoked paprika blend into a vibrant dip with a little protein and plenty of personality. Make it up to a week ahead, then serve with seeded crackers, crudités, or good bread.

Another excellent addition to the crudité platter. Hazelnuts bring out the earthy sweetness of beets, while garlic and lemon keep everything lively. Like the carrot dip above, this one can be made a week ahead.

A jar of olives, a block of feta, and some garlicky olive oil: That’s nearly all you need for this bright, briny appetizer. Have some crusty bread handy for the flavorful oil left in the bowl.

Yuzu kosho gives these deviled eggs a jolt of citrusy heat, while pickled shallots, fresh herbs, and thinly sliced radishes bring brightness and crunch. Arrange them on shiso leaves for an especially striking holiday appetizer.

A bowl of party nuts is never a bad idea, particularly when they’re seasoned with chile powder, fried curry leaves, and crispy onions. Set these out while the turkey finishes roasting.

A tangy, Parmesan-rich dressing clings to crisp-tender green beans, with pickled shallots bringing a sharp little kick. All the satisfaction of a proper Thanksgiving side, without the casserole dish.

Crispy onions are the crown on this roasted squash side; pomegranate seeds are the jewels. Add fresh herbs and a swoop of lemony yogurt, and you’ve got a dish worthy of the center of the table.

These collards aren’t cooked into submission. Simmered until just tender, they stay pleasantly substantial beneath a sharp mustard vinaigrette. Tarragon and sweet-salty walnuts finish this fresh take on a holiday greens side.

When the oven is too crowded for green bean casserole, make this stovetop alternative. Browned mushrooms, crisp-tender green beans, butter, and frizzled shallots deliver plenty of familiar holiday flavor.

One BA reader calls this their signature Thanksgiving sprouts recipe. Separating the individual leaves takes patience, but the payoff is worth it: tender-crisp greens with lots of caramelized edges.

Toss sprouts with spicy, nutty gochujang brown butter. Or, for something simpler, go for classic roasted brussels sprouts.

Coconut milk gives this bubbling, breadcrumb-topped vegan gratin its creamy consistency without any dairy. A little lemon zest and nutmeg round things out.

White miso gives these glazed carrots a deep savoriness, while scallion gremolata adds freshness. You can cook the carrots a day ahead and loosen the glaze with a splash of water when reheating.

Maple syrup plays up carrots’ natural sweetness, while a pinch of chile flakes keeps the glaze from going full candy. This is a classic Thanksgiving side with just enough heat to keep things interesting.

Or skip cooking the carrots altogether. Shave them into thin ribbons, let salt soften them slightly, then toss with sticky dates and an orange vinaigrette. Sweet, tart, crunchy, and fresh.

Blanch, smash, and dress the beans up to 12 hours ahead so they can soak up the lemony sumac vinaigrette. Finish with Asian pear, parsley, and crunchy pumpkin seeds just before serving.

Silken tofu gives this steakhouse classic its creamy texture without dairy. Aromatics add savory depth, making it a satisfying side to serve alongside turkey, stuffing, and potatoes.

Bitter greens, tangy heat, and salty crunch are especially welcome among Thanksgiving’s softer sides. Toss tender broccoli rabe with garlicky onions and pickled cherry peppers, then shower the lot with crisp Pecorino breadcrumbs.

The French bistro classic gets a holiday-friendly update: Cut the leeks into rounds rather than long stalks, making them easier to serve to a crowd. A sharp vinaigrette, toasted walnuts, and fresh tarragon finish the dish.

Steamed broccolini gets a salty-sweet dressing of tahini, miso, soy sauce, and mirin, then a scattering of lemon and sesame seeds. Make the sauce a day ahead to take one more task off your Thanksgiving list.

Sweet roasted beets meet tart grapefruit, sharp shallots, and sizzling rosemary. The colors alone could wake up a Thanksgiving spread. Plus, you can roast and peel the beets up to two days ahead.

Inspired by Cantonese steamed fish, this squash side gets a generous pouf of frizzled scallions. Ginger and chile bring the heat, turning a humble vegetable into something special.

Bharta is a Bangladeshi preparation of seasoned meat or mashed vegetables. This roasted squash version gets its punch from mustard oil, chiles, spices, and fresh cilantro.

Raw cranberries keep their tart snap in this bright relish, while toasted walnuts, mustard seeds, Fresno chile, and a little maple syrup bring crunch, heat, and sweetness. Make it up to four days ahead.

A quick parboil and a vigorous shake rough up the surfaces of these potatoes, helping them develop exceptionally crunchy crusts in the oven. The fluffy centers are practically made for soaking up gravy.

Baking potatoes instead of boiling them concentrates their flavor, while roasted garlic adds savory depth. With just six tablespoons of butter for four pounds of potatoes, this creamy mash is a little less indulgent than many holiday versions.

Steaming sweet potatoes makes their flesh especially soft and fluffy, ready for generous smears of tahini butter. Lime juice, soy sauce, and sesame oil make the flavors especially dynamic, and a welcome savory counterpoint to classic sweet potato casserole.

Thin rounds of sweet potato are arranged upright in concentric circles, then roasted with harissa until tender and crisp-edged. A crunchy dukkah of pistachios, sesame, and fennel seeds finishes this striking holiday side.

This gluten-free stuffing skips the usual process of baking cornbread, cubing it, and drying it out. Instead, mushrooms, kale, and herbs bake right into the batter.

Chewy wild rice, tossed with sautéed leeks, toasted pecans, and fresh herbs, makes a stunningly delicious (and gluten-free) alternative to traditional Thanksgiving stuffing.

If you’re firmly Team Dark Meat, these stock-braised turkey legs are the ticket. The meat becomes tender enough to pull from the bone, making for especially good leftover sandwiches the next day.

Prefer white meat, or feeding a smaller crowd? A bone-in turkey breast delivers juicy, flavorful slices without the work of roasting a whole bird. No basting or oversized roasting pan required.

Or give a whole roasted salmon fillet the holiday treatment with a crunchy salsa of toasted nuts, garlic, chile, and vinegar. Showered with fresh mint and cilantro, it’s a striking centerpiece with plenty of protein.

A crisp, golden shell of saffron rice gives way to spiced chickpeas, caramelized onions, and tart dried cherries. Crown the whole thing with a bracingly fresh herb salad for a vegetarian centerpiece everyone will love.

For a meatless main with all the ceremony of a holiday roast, this homemade tofu loaf gets filled with savory mushroom-pecan stuffing and brushed with a smoky maple-soy glaze. Pass the mushroom gravy alongside.

Tearing roasted sweet potatoes into rough chunks creates more surface area for charring and catching a spicy maple-soy glaze. Serve them over tangy lentils with scallions and pistachios for a substantial plant-based main.

A mixture of mushrooms, pearl onions, carrots, and red wine makes a rich, deeply savory vegetarian braise. Serve it over mashed potatoes or polenta, with crispy mushrooms scattered over the top.

Transform humble cabbage into a deeply flavorful vegetarian centerpiece. Here, it caramelizes while slowly braising in a spiced tomato broth. Serve the tender wedges over grains to make the meal more substantial.

Almond flour makes these warmly spiced cake layers exceptionally tender, while shredded carrots, walnuts, golden raisins, and coconut bring texture to every bite. Tangy cream cheese–Greek yogurt frosting seals the deal. Make it up to three days ahead.

Whole wheat flour and oats bring subtle nuttiness to this apple crisp, while brown sugar and butter help the topping turn golden. Serve warm, with vanilla ice cream for anyone who wants it.

This Spanish almond cake gets a seasonal turn with chopped pears and plenty of citrus zest. Naturally gluten-free and dairy-free, it’s lovely after dinner—and just as welcome with coffee the next morning.

Rich chocolate mousse gets a crackly crown of sweet sesame brittle. Serve it in individual glasses for a holiday-party-worthy capper that’s entirely vegan—and a little different from the usual parade of Thanksgiving desserts.

Golden turmeric, fragrant spices, and coconut milk give this custard pie its silky filling. The almond, oat, and coconut crust is naturally gluten-free, making the finished dessert suitable for guests avoiding both gluten and dairy.

A platter of seasonal citrus—think grapefruit, mandarin oranges, and whatever else looks good at the market—gets a crunchy topping of pistachios, almonds, pumpkin seeds, and toasted coconut.

#6564. A Virtual Lifeless Earth Will Help Scientists Find Life on Exoplanets

In the search for life elsewhere in the galaxy, astronomers sift through exoplanet discoveries looking for ones that could be habitable. That means rocky planets with atmospheres in habitable zones. But one thing stymies these efforts. Can we examine atmospheres and differentiate between an exoplanet that's habitable and one that's actually inhabited?

That's difficult, partly because exoplanets are so far away, and also because we only have Earth to guide us. It's the only habitable and inhabited world we know of. But new research shows how we can work with those facts to try to detect inhabited worlds.

The work is "A Whole-planet Model of the Earth without Life for Terrestrial Exoplanet Studies," and it's published in The Planetary Science Journal. The lead author is Samantha Gilbert-Janizek, who was a postdoctoral astronomy student at the University of Washington when conducting this work.

"As the only known habitable (and inhabited) planet in the Universe, Earth informs our search for life elsewhere," the authors write. "Future telescopes like the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) will soon look for life on rocky worlds around Sun-like stars, so it is critical that we understand how to distinguish habitable planets from inhabited planets."

Observatories like the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) will inject new energy into the search for life. They will shift exoplanet science from identifying worlds that could be habitable, to identifying worlds with atmospheres showing signs of life. But as the researchers point out, we still don't know how to tell inhabited worlds, if there are any, from those that are merely habitable.

"Earth is currently the only known inhabited planet in the Universe, and geological evidence suggests that it was habitable with liquid-water oceans for most of its 4.54 Gyr history," the authors write. "Owing to its long-term habitability, Earth serves as the template that guides our search for biospheres elsewhere."

The researchers tackled this issue by building a sort of virtual Earth, but one without life.

"As a first step toward answering these questions, we present a coupled interior-atmosphere evolution model of the Earth without life from 50 Myr to 5 Gyr that reproduces 19 key observations of the preindustrial Earth after 4.5 Gyr within estimated measurement uncertainties," the researchers explain. Those 19 observations included atmospheric CO2 and H2O, surface temperature and albedo, ocean mass, and even factors like upper-mantle temperature and upper-mantle heat flow. These non-biological factors all shape a planet's atmosphere and have to be accounted for.

"Though exoplanet interiors themselves will likely never be directly observable, the effects of interior evolution are apparent in the composition of the atmosphere and the albedo of the surface environment, both of which HWO will observe on Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars via reflected-light spectroscopy," the authors explain.

This schematic shows some of the key processes included in the abiotic Earth model. Remotely observable quantities (surface temperature, albedo, and atmospheric H2O and CO2) are in bold. Image Credit: Samantha Gilbert-Janizek et al 2026 Planet. Sci. J. 7 216

The researchers also produced reflected light spectra of the model Earth that covers the likely wavelength range of the HWO. They used a code to compute a "synthetic HWO reflected-light spectra (0.2â2.0 Î¼m) for the true Earth and the abiotic Earthâs atmospheric state after 4.5 Gyr," the authors write. These included line absorptions for CO2, H2O, O2, O3, and CH4.

This virtual Earth without life can serve as a benchmark to compare with detailed atmosphere observations of habitable worlds.

âThis model can help us see how habitable but non-living planets might mimic living planets,â lead author Gilbert-Janizek said. "When we interpret observations of an exoplanetâs atmosphere, this tool will help us determine the probability that what we observe indicates life on the surface.â

This schematic shows the atmospheric sources and sinks that define the new volatile cycling processes in the model. Fluxes related to CO2 are color-coded magenta, and fluxes related to H2O are color-coded teal. The schematic doesn't include ocean chemistry. Image Credit: Samantha Gilbert-Janizek et al 2026 Planet. Sci. J. 7 216

Gilbert-Janizek didn't start from scratch. Senior author Rory Barnes, a UW associate professor of astronomy, had already built a model that included the core, mantle, crust and stellar radiation. This work added the surface and the atmosphere to build a more comprehensive model.

The authors hope that this model can serve as a kind of plug-and-play model that can be adjusted to fit with any particular exoplanet being studied. They can input factors like albedo and atmospheric CO2 and test what happens. If the model then recreates the observations of the planet, it suggests that the exoplanet in question is uninhabited.

Naturally, an undertaking of this size and complexity requires some assumptions. The model initializes after Earth's magma ocean solidified, and that dictated the atmosphere's initial composition. The authors say they chose an initial set of conditions "that apply after the bulk of the mantle has solidified."

They also assumed that plate tectonics were active during all of Earth's history beginning in the middle Hadean, which is widely believed to be true and in line with evidence. There are alternative hypotheses saying that this wasn't the case. One says that plate tectonics only began when it shifted from a stagnant-lid to modern plate tectonics during the Archaean, but the researchers avoided that.

Other assumptions were made regarding atmospheric pressure, the strength of Earth's geodynamo, and even atmospheric escape of hydrogen. But these types of assumptions are a normal part of science and are explained up front.

But the virtual Earth model successfully reproduces the properties of the Pre-Industrial Earth, and that's the most important thing. It also predicts that a planet can maintain habitable conditions for a long time without requiring the presence of life. This is relevant because false positives are one of the HWO's challenges.

These are three Engineering Architecture Concepts (EACs) for the Habitable Worlds Observatory. Each one features a different mirror design. EAC-1 is a 6m, segmented, off-axis telescope. EAC-2 is the same but uses a round keystone mirror and surrounding segments. EAC-3 is an 8m on-axis telescope with round segments. Not shown is the extendable, protective barrel that each design has, which will protect the mirror from micrometeorites. Image Credit: NASA Goddard/Conceptual Image Labs

âDr. Gilbert-Janizekâs work represents an exciting step toward understanding where life can exist in the universe,â Barnes said. âAfter more than a decade of work by many scientists, Dr. Gilbert-Janizek has finally completed a model of the Earth that simultaneously reproduces properties of Earthâs core, mantle, surface and atmosphere. That calibration gives us confidence that future simulations of exoplanets will be accurate.â

The question "Are we alone in the Universe" can be asked in one breath but not answered in one. It has to be broken down to much smaller questions asked and answered across many generations. Even "Are we alone in the Milky Way" is far too large and encompassing a question. "Are we alone" has to be asked exoplanet by exoplanet, and that requires tools of the sort developed by Dr. Gilbert-Janizek and her colleagues.

Our first 6,000 exoplanet discoveries were bulk discoveries. But the search is becoming more targeted toward Earth-like planets, meaning tools like this one are becoming more and more necessary. The upcoming HWO, if it gets built, places this point in even finer focus.

âRealizing the ambitious goals of a telescope like the Habitable Worlds Observatory requires decades of work across many generations of scientists,â Gilbert-Janizek said. âIâm so grateful to join this lineage and one day pass the torch to the next generation so that we can continue chipping away at this question of whether or not we are alone in the universe.â

#6563. We’re in the Era of the $200 Cup of Coffee

Can coffee join the ranks of wine when it comes to high-end tastings?

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Starting this week, it’s also home to a $200 cup of coffee.

Bushwick’s Sey Coffee recently announced that it would be touring a rare Panamanian geisha from Finca Sophia, a coffee farm in Panama’s Chiriquí highlands. Sey scooped up the geisha at auction for $44,275, which comes to $6,325 per kilogram, or roughly $200 per cup. The geisha is billed as extraordinarily aromatic, floral, and juicy; Doug Cohen, Sey’s director of brand strategy, advises enjoying it with a clean palate, completely black, and taking your time with it. “As the coffee cools, different aspects of its character become apparent, and that evolution is part of the experience,” he says.

Even among fourth-wave coffee shops where prices continue to climb higher, Sey’s $200 cup is an outlier. “Coffee as a premium product is relatively new,” says Cohen. “For so long, coffee has been treated as a commodity, and its value has been constrained by that perception.” He says that both before and right after COVID, folks were becoming more curious about coffee, and educating themselves on platforms like Youtube, Discord, and online forums about how to appreciate it and “understand just how high the ceiling of quality can be.” The arrival of the $200 cup of coffee from a cafe in a neighborhood at the epicenter of conversations about both culinary innovation and gentrification feels ripe for closer examination.

So, how did this coffee end up at this price? “We have been purchasing coffee from Finca Sophia for several years,” Cohen says. “This release really grew out of that existing relationship.” When Finca’s general manager told Cohen that the farm’s yields were down by approximately 95 percent, Cohen says a bigger question was raised: “What does it mean to be a good partner when the people you have built relationships with are facing a difficult year?” Buying up the geisha beans felt like a way to both support Sey’s producer, and further develop what Cohen calls “elevated coffee experiences.”

In the 2010s, the artisanal coffeehouse wave washed over the country, and especially Brooklyn, with hipster gusto. Sey Coffee was an integral part of that boom. Initially called Lofted Coffee, it operated out of its founders’ Bushwick loft until it rebranded to Sey in 2017, and expanded operations to its present Bushwick location on Grattan Street. That space has become something of a local icon since; Sprudge called its aesthetic “shoebox crossed with an airplane hangar”; the minimal-industrial, cream-hued interiors hit a very Axel Vervoordt-with-a-cyber-sigil-tattoo note (positive). The shop’s cachet has drawn coffee lovers, artists, yuppies, and artist-yuppies; customers have snacked on the gluten-free pastries from L’imprimerie (and now, post-L’imprimerie closure, pastries from Smør), and often post up with their dogs thanks to the semi-indoor-outdoor layout.

Sey is hoping to elevate the coffee shop model to something more premium, with a stated focus on ethics and sustainability. Thus far, it’s earned acclaim for those efforts. Food & Wine named it the best coffee shop in New York and received positive media attention for opting out of tipping, choosing instead to pay its staff up to more than 80 percent above the NYC hourly minimum wage; full-time baristas can make up to $31 per hour in addition to receiving benefits and a share of the cafe’s revenue.

Increasingly, coffee is getting the same treatment as high-end dining and tasting experiences. There’s the omakase-style menu at NYC’s Driftaway Coffee, or San Francisco’s Komakase coffee tasting room, both of which steer coffee away from quick consumption and toward a world of degustation that appears to have more in common with pricier wine and spirit tastings. The expansion of “espresso house” chain Watch House stateside is also an indicator: The London-based specialty roaster expanded to a fourth location in New York City this summer, raising eyebrows for its $32 cup of coffee while also reportedly scouting for more locations in Austin, Chicago, and Miami.

The emerging demand may be just much about luxury as it is about craft. I can’t help but wonder if the $200 cup of coffee is happening in Bushwick because the Girls-era Bushwickian has grown up and wants more exclusive experiences. Is this what happens when, as culture writer Raven Smith said on his new BBC podcast last week, the indie outgrows its sleaze? “For us, this is not about pushing prices higher for the sake of it,” Cohen says. “It is about challenging how we assign value to coffee in the first place. What is an extraordinary coffee actually worth?”

As much as we may lament climbing prices for specialty coffee and espresso, why wouldn’t this happen to the category when so many other aspects of food and beverage — from cocktails to sushi to bread — are following the same trajectory? Higher consumer costs notwithstanding, the marketing of specialty beans does steer U.S. coffee culture away from its productivity-focused consumption and the work-optimized “coffee break.”

“Why do we accept that certain wines can command thousands of dollars, yet question whether coffee can have comparable value?” Cohen asks. It’s a fair question, albeit one that I’d answer with another: Once we acknowledge that coffee should command a higher price, who still gets to drink it?

#6562. A Devastating Disease Is Threatening the World’s Chocolate Supply – but Scientists May Have Found the Answer

A change to just two DNA letters reduced disease in cacao by about 42% under laboratory conditions, suggesting a possible way to protect future chocolate harvests.

Black pod disease is estimated to reduce cacao yields by roughly 30% worldwide, threatening the livelihoods of farmers who grow the crop used to make chocolate. Shifting weather patterns and other environmental stresses are making production even more difficult. With millions of farmers depending on cacao, these pressures are raising concerns about the future of the global chocolate supply.

Scientists at Penn State have developed a new variety of cacao that shows significantly improved resistance to black pod disease in laboratory tests. The researchers used gene editing and traditional breeding to strengthen the plant’s natural defenses, offering a potential way to reduce losses without introducing foreign DNA into the final plant. The promising results are now moving toward field testing and possible commercial production.

The work builds on decades of research led by Mark Guiltinan, the J. Franklin Styer Professor of Horticultural Botany and professor of plant molecular biology in the Department of Plant Sciences at Penn State’s College of Agricultural Sciences, and Siela Maximova, a research professor of plant biotechnology in the same department.

“For consumers, chocolate is something they expect to find on store shelves every day, but behind that product is a crop and industry facing significant challenges,” Guiltinan said. “Our goal is to develop tools that help growers continue producing cacao sustainably and profitably.”

Cacao is particularly vulnerable to environmental changes because of where it evolved. Native to the Amazon rainforest, the species originally grew beneath the canopy of tropical forests, where surrounding trees helped create relatively stable conditions. Today, cacao is cultivated across tropical regions of Africa, Asia, and Latin America, often in environments quite different from its original habitat.

“Cacao evolved in a very stable rainforest environment,” Guiltinan said. “It’s a delicate plant in many ways. Changes in rainfall, temperature, and humidity can all affect production, and some of those changes can also increase disease pressure.”

These environmental pressures are especially concerning because cacao trees cannot be improved quickly through traditional breeding. A tree takes roughly three years to mature and begin producing seeds, and developing and evaluating a new variety can take decades. Meanwhile, changing weather conditions, including increased humidity and variability, can create more favorable conditions for pathogens and insect pests.

“The climate is changing faster than these trees can naturally adapt,” Maximova said. “One of our goals is to develop tools that help breeders respond more quickly to those challenges.”

In a study published in the Plant Biotechnology Journal, the team combined genome sequencing, CRISPR gene editing, and traditional crossbreeding to develop cacao plants with greater resistance to black pod disease. The disease is caused by a mold-like pathogen that attacks cacao plants and can severely reduce harvests.

The researchers targeted a gene called TcNPR3, which normally acts as a brake on the plant’s immune system. By changing this gene, they partially activated the cacao tree’s natural defense response, giving it greater protection against subsequent pathogen infections.

The genetic change was remarkably small. Rather than introducing a completely new defense system, the scientists adjusted one already present in the plant. After making the edit, they used traditional breeding to remove all transgenic material, including the foreign DNA associated with the gene-editing machinery. The resulting plants retained the beneficial change without carrying foreign DNA.

This distinction is important for how the plants are regulated. According to the researchers, the resulting cacao is no longer considered a genetically modified organism, or GMO, consistent with U.S. and European Union regulatory frameworks that treat certain gene-edited traits similarly to those produced through conventional breeding.

“In one case, we only changed two bases in the entire genome of the plant,” Guiltinan said. “Out of roughly 450 million bases, that single change resulted in about a 42% reduction in disease under laboratory conditions.”

That result provides encouraging evidence that a small genetic adjustment can improve cacao’s disease defenses. However, laboratory conditions cannot fully reproduce the environmental challenges trees encounter on farms, and the researchers have not yet established whether the same protection will hold under commercial growing conditions.

Field evaluations are now underway through collaborations with the U.S. Department of Agriculture in Hawaii and Puerto Rico. These trials will help determine how the edited plants perform in actual growing environments before decisions are made about broader cultivation.

“These plants are specifically designed to improve disease resistance,” Maximova said. “The next step is proving performance in field trials. Scale-up and marketing will be the next challenges should the field testing prove encouraging. That’s where commercial partners can play an important role in helping move the technology forward.”

Penn State has recently entered into a licensing agreement with AgroNetica, a biotechnology company focused on cacao, to advance that process. The company has licensed the commercial rights to plants carrying the disease-tolerance mutation and plans to continue testing, expand production, and eventually market improved cacao varieties directly to growers in cacao-producing countries.

Turning a successful laboratory experiment into a crop that farmers can reliably grow requires considerably more than demonstrating that the genetic modification works. Plants must undergo additional testing, be produced in sufficient quantities, and reach growers through commercial distribution systems. Universities generally lack the resources needed to carry out that entire process.

“It takes millions of dollars and many years to bring a new crop variety to farmers,” Maximova said. “That’s why partnerships with companies willing to invest in development, testing and deployment are so important.”

The agreement also marks a milestone for Penn State’s Program in the Molecular Biology of Cocoa, which Guiltinan and Maximova co-direct. The program traces its origins to an industry-supported endowment established in the 1980s. Over the following decades, Penn State researchers developed foundational tools for cacao biotechnology, mapped important genetic pathways, and established one of the world’s leading cacao research programs.

Those advances created the scientific foundation for the current gene-editing work. They also demonstrate why maintaining a research program over many years can be necessary before discoveries become practical agricultural technologies.

“Thanks to this long-term investment in research and maintaining a sustained program, we now have an opportunity to begin getting technologies developed here in the lab closer to the hands of farmers,” Maximova said. “The focus was always on helping cacao farmers and the industry. We’re now at the place where we have a partner whose expertise is moving these discoveries into real-world use.”

Disease resistance is only one of the traits that researchers and commercial developers hope to improve. AgroNetica also plans to introduce additional characteristics from its development pipeline, including greater tolerance to heat and drought, reduced cadmium accumulation, and more compact trees that could allow greater mechanization. Other goals include shortening the time before a tree’s first harvest and developing caffeine-free cacao varieties. These remain development objectives rather than demonstrated benefits of the newly licensed disease-tolerant plants.

Guiltinan and Maximova are continuing to investigate traits associated with climate resilience and crop productivity. They expect accelerated breeding and genome editing to play increasingly important roles in helping cacao growers respond to environmental pressures that may change throughout the lifetime of a tree.

“The diseases are changing. The climate is changing. The challenges growers face continue to evolve,” Maximova said. “This is not something you solve once, and then you’re finished. It’s an ongoing effort to develop better plants and provide growers with new options.”

For Guiltinan, the success of the research will ultimately depend on whether these advances translate into meaningful improvements for the people growing cacao.

“We’re trying to solve real problems for farmers,” he said. “If we can help growers reduce losses, improve productivity and adapt more quickly to changing conditions, then that’s the ultimate measure of success.”

Reference: “Reduced Susceptibility to Phytophthora in Non-Transgenic Cacao Progeny Through CRISPR–Cas9 Mediated TcNPR3 Mutagenesis” by Mark J. Guiltinan, Lena Landherr, Siela N. Maximova, Dante DelVecchio, Aswathy Sebastian and Istvan Albert, 9 September 2025, Plant Biotechnology Journal. DOI: 10.1111/pbi.70365

Satellite radar and underground electrical scans have revealed a 2,600-year-old structure at Buto, one of ancient Egypt's most sacred cities. The real surprise wasn't the walls — but what was underneath them.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Egyptian researchers have found a hidden 2,600-year-old structure the size of a football field after using satellites to peer below the ground. But what they found beneath the structure may be just as remarkable as the building itself.

The site they examined is known as Buto (modern-day Tell el-Fara'in), a sprawling mound of layered history in the northwestern Nile Delta. To the ancient Egyptians, it was the sacred home of Wadjet, the cobra goddess of Lower Egypt, and one of the most religiously important cities in the pharaonic landscape.

Archaeologists have excavated its upper layers for decades, finding remains from the rule of the Macedonian Ptolemaic dynasty (305 to 30 B.C.) and Roman era (30 B.C. to A.D. 395). But the deeper, older layers at the site — including a mound called Kom C, sitting below groundwater level in waterlogged delta clay — had stayed stubbornly out of reach. Kom C itself rises above the surface as a visible mound, but earlier excavations had reached only the Ptolemaic and Roman layers before hitting the water table.

Now, researchers have turned to noninvasive tools, including satellite imagery, to delve into the mysterious subterranean layers.

First, they turned to the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 satellite, which can produce radar images by beaming down microwave pulses from orbit and then measuring how they reflect back; the returning signals can reveal subtle differences in surface moisture, elevation and reflectivity that can hint at buried structures beneath the ground. After looking at these radar images, the team spotted a large oval-shaped anomaly buried beneath Kom C that was 420 feet long and 203 feet wide (128 by 62 meters).

The geological profile of Tell el-Fara'in (ancient Buto) and the surrounding Nile Delta, showing the layered sequence of river sands and flood-plain clays from the last ice age and the settlement mound above.

To learn more without disturbing the site, the team ran 15 parallel lines of electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) across an area of roughly 58,100 square feet (5,400 square meters). This technique reveals the underground landscape by passing electrical currents through the earth, measuring how they travel and creating a map that archaeologists can read.

The picture that came back was layered. Between the surface and 10 feet (3 m) down, the team found scattered Ptolemaic and Roman debris, including displaced mudbricks, pottery shards and broken limestone, which point to centuries of continued occupation and rebuilding on the site. Later residents dismantled older structures for reuse and left a scatter of displaced material behind.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Using pure sand as a stabilizing cushion was a brilliant, deliberate tactic — the ancient builders profoundly understood their environment.

Deeper still, between 10 and 20 feet (3 and 6 m), the researchers found a large mudbrick structure from the 26th dynasty (688 to 525 B.C.), also known as the Saite period. They were able to date this discovery based on its layer, the unique shape of the mudbricks and other artifacts such as pottery, which the team dated by style and their archaeological layer, with carbon-14 dating applied to associated organic material. The large structure may be a tomb, a house for priests or a religious shrine, the team wrote in the study, published in March in the journal Acta Geophysica.

And below that, at 20 to 23 feet (6 to 7 m) underground, the researchers unexpectedly found a thick, clean layer of sand.

That sand is the discovery within the discovery, the team wrote in the study.

The Nile Delta's clay is notoriously treacherous to build on. It absorbs moisture and swells, and then contracts and shifts as it dries — posing a slow-motion threat to anything heavy sitting on top of it. The Saite builders, it seems, knew this. Before laying the foundations to their structure, they packed a cushion of clean sand beneath it. This sand would have spread the building's weight, let groundwater drain through, and stopped the clay from creeping. It is the same logic behind modern load-distributing foundations — applied here more than two and a half millennia ago.

A 2D electrical resistivity scan aligned with a partially exposed mudbrick wall — the colored subsurface anomaly matches the location of the visible structure above ground.

"By combining satellite radar with deep ERT profiles, we didn't just map the walls of this massive Saite-era structure — we were also able to analyze the subsurface layers," study co-author author Abdelaziz Elfadaly, an associate research professor at Egypt's National Authority for Remote Sensing and Space Sciences, told Live Science. "The detection of a significant, clean sand foundation layer beneath the mudbrick walls explains how these heavy structures survived the high water table and shifting clayey soil of Buto."

The sand layer, in effect, acts as a barrier; it stops groundwater from wicking upward into the mudbrick, which would soften and dissolve it. The sand also lets water drain sideways instead of pooling against the foundation, according to Elfadaly.

A 3-by-3 foot (10 by 10 m) excavation trench that was around 20 to 23 feet (6 to 7 m) deep confirmed the presence of thick mudbrick walls resting on that sand layer, and nearby, a spread of objects that hint at the site's sacred function. According to Elfadaly, these finds included ushabti and shawabti figurines — small servant statues typically placed in tombs to serve the deceased in the afterlife — and a limestone altar whose carved channels bore dried residues consistent with animal blood, pointing to offering rituals performed at the site. The study also noted a rarer find: a faience baboon figurine, the kind associated with Thoth, the god of wisdom.

Image credit: Abouarab et al.,Acta Geophysica (2026); CC BY 4.0

Layout of the ERT (electrical resistivity tomography) survey at Kom C. The blue lines mark one first set of profiles, and the red lines mark the second. Insets show the electrodes and cables deployed in the field, and a large mudbrick wall dating to the Late Roman period.

Image credit: Abouarab et al.,Acta Geophysica (2026); CC BY 4.0

A selection of artifacts recovered from the excavated square at Kom C, including small figurines and worked stone fragments from the Saite-era structure.

The Saite period was a moment of cultural revival. After generations of Assyrian and Libyan domination, Egyptian pharaohs retook the throne and poured resources into restoring Egypt's religious landscape, particularly in the Nile Delta, which had been their power base. Buto, with its deep ties to Lower Egyptian identity, was a natural focus. The Saite kings ruled from the nearby delta city of Sais, so restoring Buto reinforced their roots and their claim to the throne.

"A monumental building of this scale underscores the Saite pharaohs' intense commitment to glorifying the Delta region," Hussein Bassir, director of the Antiquities Museum at a cultural research center known as Bibliotheca Alexandrina who wasn't involved with the study, told Live Science in a WhatsApp message. "Using pure sand as a stabilizing cushion was a brilliant, deliberate tactic — the ancient builders profoundly understood their environment."

The team is planning a return visit, this time using wider-spaced electrical resistivity surveys to reach deeper layers, along with specialists who study ancient plants and also understand how geological features changed over time, which may help reconstruct what the landscape around Buto looked like when these walls were first laid.

Abouarab, M. a. R., Elfadaly, A., Elbehery, W., Wafa, O., Aboalkassim, I., Younes, A., Hiekl, A. M. A., Saada, S. A., Wilson, P., & Ibrahim, A. (2026). Multi-scale detection of buried archaeological elements across different occupation phases: an integrated approach using radar satellite imagery and electric resistivity tomography at Buto, northwestern Nile Delta of Egypt. Acta Geophysica, 74(2). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11600-026-01809-4

Wafaa Tantawy is an Egyptian archaeologist and heritage conservation specialist who graduated from Cairo University. She specializes in archaeological conservation and ancient Egyptian material culture, and brings firsthand field experience from Egyptian archaeological sites. Her work has been published on Ancient Origins and Medium, where she focuses on making Egypt's rich archaeological record accessible to global audiences.

#6560. Giant Impacts Help Rocky Planets Retain Their Atmospheres

Earth's formation was a messy process. It all happened about 4.5 billion years ago, in our young chaotic Solar System. Rocky planetesimals were whizzing around in the Solar System back then, and Earth formed as more of these objects collided and merged with it.

Some of these collisions were giant impacts that generated immense heat. These were common in the later stages of Earth's formation, after the protoplanetary disk had largely dissipated and atmospheric accretion was complete. Planetary scientists have wondered how young planets like Earth could've held onto their atmospheres near the end of their accretion period. The massive heat from giant impacts should've driven primordial He/H atmospheres away. But new research suggests that simple picture doesn't capture some important details, and that giant impacts could've actually helped young rocky planets retain their atmospheres.

The work is titled "Retention of primordial atmospheres through giant impacts," and it's published in Nature Astronomy. The authors are Darius Modirrousta-Galian and Jun Korenaga. Modirrousta-Galian is a former Yale postdoc who is now at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and Korenaga is a professor of Earth and planetary sciences in Yaleâs Faculty of Arts and Sciences.

This research focuses on what happens near the end of a rocky planet's accretion process, after the protoplanetary disk has largely dissipated. This is when other planetesimals had also grown large through their own accretion processes, and when they collided with a planet like Earth, they released an enormous amount of energy.

âGiant impacts are a key part of how rocky planets grow,â said co-author Korenaga. âPlanets the size of Earth or larger are expected to form through collisions between smaller planetary bodies. These collisions add mass and release enormous amounts of heat, which can drive atmospheric escape. Their effect on a planetâs atmosphere depends on how those two changes work together.â

Modirrousta-Galian and Korenaga have been working on how planetary interiors and atmospheres evolve together and have published several papers on the topic. Their previous research laid the foundation for this work.

Their work shows that increased heat near a planet's surface isn't the only result of impacts. Some of that heat is driven deep into the planet. The impact can also "increase atmospheric gravitational binding," according to the researchers.

There are two components of a giant impact: heat and mass.

This illustration shows planetesimals in a disk around a young star. Rocky planets grow by accretion of planetesimals, and as time goes on, the planetesimals become more massive. When these massive planetesimals impact young planets, they not only generate heat, they add mass. Image Credit: NASA / JPL-Caltech.

When a planetesimal smashes into a rocky planet, the heat can be divided into two separate components. Some of it is driven more deeply into the planet where it won't drive away the atmosphere. Some of it will be mantle heat that does contribute to driving the primordial atmosphere away. But the mass gained by the accretion of the planetesimal isn't divided. All of that mass gives the planet more power to hold onto its atmosphere.

"Whereas the entire accreted mass contributes to the increase in gravitational binding energy, only part of the impact energy raises mantle temperature," the authors explain. "Mantle melting consumes energy as latent heat, while the impactorâs metallic core transfers little energy to the mantle and remains superheated at depth."

"Giant impacts therefore increase gravitational binding energy more than mantle thermal energy, shifting planets towards atmospheric retention," the researchers explain.

This understanding can help explain the exoplanet population.

Astronomers used to think that our Solar System was an archetype of how other solar systems would look. There would be rocky planets in the inner Solar System, gas giants further out, and ice giants beyond them. But exoplanet discoveries have cast doubt on that. The most common types of detected exoplanets aren't even represented in our Solar System: super-Earths and sub-Neptunes.

Astronomers think that super-Earths and sub-Neptunes could represent two types of planets that started out as rocky cores but ended up with much different atmospheres. Super-Earths have lost their atmospheres, while sub-Neptunes have retained more of their primordial atmospheres. A sub-Neptune only needs to retain a few percent of its H/He atmosphere to have an extended puffy atmosphere that can increase its radius by a large amount.

These are artist's impressions of the super-Earth Kepler-452b (right) and the sub-Neptune Kepler-22b (left). They're very different from each other, and both types of exoplanet are abundant in exoplanet discoveries. Giant impacts could explain their abundance. Image Credit: NASA.

âWhy nature produces both types in such abundance is a fundamental puzzle in exoplanetary science,â said Modirrousta-Galian. âWe set out to find an explanation.â

This research shows that sub-Neptunes could have grown larger through more massive impacts, and those impacts not only added mass but allowed them to retain larger atmospheres. Super-Earth's weren't subjected to those same massive impacts, and so did not gain enough mass to retain their atmospheres the same way that sub-Neptunes did. They lost theirs due to stellar radiation.

This schematic shows different outcomes for rocky planets. In one scenario, massive impacts onto a rocky create a more massive planet that can retain more of its primordial atmosphere: a sub-Neptune. In the other scenario, there are no massive impacts, no increase in rocky mass, and the planet retains less of its atmosphere. Image Credit: Darius Modirrousta-Galian

"Larger, atmosphere-bearing planets emerge preferentially through collisional growth," the researchers explain. "By contrast, smaller planets without such impacts tend to lose their primordial atmospheres under sustained stellar irradiation. At the population level, these results suggest that sub-Neptunes have, on average, more massive rocky interiors than super-Earths."

These results appear to overturn the long-held idea that giant impacts spelled doom for planetary atmospheres, and in turn, for the prospects of habitability. Primordial H/He atmospheres themselves didnt create habitability. But some research shows that they're essential for the development of a world that is eventually habitable, through interactions with a young rocky planet's magma ocean. These interactions may have been a significant source of Earth's water and could be on other rocky worlds, too.

âThis overturns the decades-old canonical view that giant impacts almost always lead to complete atmospheric loss, demonstrating instead that these collisions can play a crucial role in the formation of sub-Neptunes,â Korenaga said.

Evan Gough is a science-loving guy with no formal education who loves Earth, forests, hiking, and heavy music. He's guided by Carl Sagan's quote: "Understanding is a kind of ecstasy."

#6559. Steal My Food Itinerary: 3 Days on Prince Edward Island

Canada’s smallest province is big on fresh produce, pristine seafood, gorgeous views, and warm conviviality.

Recently I spent a few days exploring Prince Edward Island, a place that embraces its local foodways with gusto. There’s a complex history here, with roots in Indigenous Mi’kmaq, Acadian, Irish, Scottish, and other cultures. And if one thing unites these histories, it’s the island’s abundance of seafood and produce, which have helped earn it the nickname Canada’s Food Island. How can you not want to visit Canada’s Food Island?

On a stretch of land only about 140 miles long, you can eat oysters pulled out of nearby waters, potatoes grown on local farms, dig into a juicy burger made with PEI beef, and lick ice cream made with milk from the cows you pass along those famous red-dirt roads. That’s a lot of good eating packed into a place you can drive across in an afternoon.

I had to structure my visit, therefore, around where to dine, but also include a bucket-list visit to Green Gables Heritage Place. (I am a complete freak for L.M. Montgomery’s novel Anne of Green Gables, set on PEI around the turn of the last century.) I also had to schedule time at the PEI International Shellfish Festival, which promised endless trays of freshly shucked oysters and clams, hot buttered lobster rolls, steaming bowls of mussels, and plenty of entertainment, from shucking competitions and cooking demos to live music and dancing.

My husband and I rented a car and stationed ourselves in Charlottetown, the island’s main hub. Prince Edward Island is situated in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, just a hop away from Nova Scotia. You’re never far from the ocean here, and on a sunny day, the air seems to sparkle. The island is known for its red-sand cliffs and beaches, rolling landscapes, fishing harbors, and lighthouses. If you’ve read Anne of Green Gables, you’ll know just how pretty PEI is.

We landed late Thursday afternoon, ready to hit the ground running. With just shy of three days, I had carefully mapped out the places I wanted to visit, using Charlottetown as my base.

Charlottetown isn’t big, and most things here are walkable within 20 minutes or so. First stop in PEI: Slaymaker & Nichols, a gastropub and inn with the feel of an old-fashioned supper club. It takes its name from the 19th-century circus that once performed on the site. They take cocktail making seriously here. The summery feel of the day prompted me to try the watermelon mule, with hibiscus-infused vodka and chunks of pickled watermelon. I liked it, especially alongside the creamy lobster dip with tomatoes and harissa, and the buttery shrimp pil pil, with lots of tasty little spears of asparagus.

I was saving myself for my first lobster roll, which we grabbed up the street in an unremarkable spot. It was pretty mediocre, so I won’t go on about it. But after eating, we stopped into Reddins, a speakeasy that channels PEI’s Prohibition history in a dark, intimate third-floor bar with vintage furniture, good jazz, and whimsical cocktails. Our excellent bartender, AB, told us the space had once been a pharmacy where folks came during Prohibition to get their “medicine” — drugstores could legally dispense alcohol by prescription. We tried a few of the signature cocktails, and the one that stood out was the Pink Canary, with vodka, rose, lychee, citrus, and rosé bubbles, served in a small bathtub. Yup, you heard that right. It was sweet and awfully fun to sip.

Tip: You need a secret password to get in when you buzz from downstairs. You can get it online, or just do as we did and ask the hostess next door for help.

In the pouring rain, we made our way to nearby Victoria Row for breakfast at local roaster Receiver Coffee. Fuel for the day included strong coffee, a particularly good cup of Earl Grey cream tea, and the Ham Slam, a big fluffy cheddar biscuit layered with a runny fried egg, Black Forest ham, Swiss, and Dijon mayo.

We swung by the shellfish festival (more on that later) but the rain wasn’t welcoming, so we got back in the car and drove out to tiny and charming Victoria-by-the-Sea. When I say tiny, I mean it: The town is half a square mile, with a population under 200. Despite the town’s size, Landmark Oyster House, set there in an old general store with pretty green shingles and a steep gabled roof, thrives.

Our friendly waiter (everyone is abundantly friendly on PEI) suggested Raspberry Point oysters to start. They hit the spot: medium-sized, briny, and sweet, served with lemon wedges and freshly grated horseradish, which is now how I think every oyster should be eaten. We also tried the scallop dog, with buttery sweet scallops, bacon jam, red pepper aioli, and pickled shallots nestled in a toasted bun. It came alongside a very good, eggy potato salad.

After seeing the cheery lighthouse and visiting a couple of little gift shops, we popped into Island Chocolates, a family-run shop and café where bars and truffles are hand-crafted, often using local ingredients like haskap, a berry that tastes somewhere between a blueberry and raspberry. That fruity haskap truffle had a nice thick shell of milk chocolate.

Sun out? Check. We spent the afternoon at the festival and got a substantial fix of oysters and clams. The lobster rolls here were stuffed with unadorned lobster meat, then melted butter from a gigantic vat was ladled over the top.

For dinner, both our bartender and waiter at Slaymaker recommended North Shore Canteen in French River, a local haunt for sure. (A slew of chefs from the shellfish festival were two tables down from us.) The menu, which changes with the current haul, hit on the day’s best ingredients: halibut, striped bass, the aforementioned shellfish, beef, and potatoes. We opted for a very generous portion of local beef tartare, amazingly tasty with capers, roasted garlic, and freshly grated Parmesan, served with Covered Bridge potato chips. We wanted to try more PEI beef and opted for a juicy hanger steak with chimichurri and black garlic, which showcased it well. Dessert was a must: parsnip cake drizzled with caramel sauce for the win.

It was time for me to check Green Gables off my bucket list. This is an article about where to eat, so suffice it to say that if you’re a fan, this is 100 percent worth a visit to see the house, wander the Haunted Wood and Lover’s Lane, and taste some nonalcoholic raspberry cordial (IYKYK).

All that walking made me hungry, which was good because this was a much anticipated two-lunch day.

First stop: Blue Mussel Café, a bright and very welcoming, beloved PEI restaurant set just back from the water in Rustico Harbor. I think it’s obvious what to order, and for good reason: These are excellent mussels — plump, fresh, and brought to the table piled high in a large stainless steel bowl. You can have them prepared with rosemary and lemon or beer and wine. I’d rate them equally, but I did like the hit of rosemary. Melted butter comes in a small ramekin on the side; I used it to dip each mussel, and my husband poured it all over the top. I didn’t have it, but the other signature, seafood chowder, looked popular. It’s made with haddock, salmon, scallops, mussels, and PEI potatoes, and served with a giant biscuit. Noted for my next visit.

We hightailed it to our next meal because I had yet to have the perfect lobster roll. Richard’s Fresh Seafood in Covehead Wharf delivered. This is one of the island’s longest-running fish shacks, where you can savor fish and chips and beer on the deck overlooking the fishing boats, or camp out on the nearby beach under the lighthouse with a lobster roll. no mistake: This is the quintessential lobster roll. It was an exercise in abundance, packed with sweet lobster meat that managed to be chunky and fine, bound with lemon and chive mayo and tiny bits of onion, all stuffed in a buttery toasted bun. It came with crunchy coleslaw, crispy fries, and a paper cup of ketchup. There are other menu items, but this lobster roll alone is worth the trip to PEI.

For our final dinner, we drove back toward North Rustico Harbor to Rustico Cannery, which opened this past spring. The airy, modern space has giant windows and a big deck that takes in super sunset views.

I needed greens, and Rustico delivered. We had crisp romaine hearts with a creamy, spicy charred jalapeño dressing, lardons, Parmesan, and sourdough crunchies. My husband hit the jackpot with his dinner: panko crusted, pan-fried haddock with pickled beet remoulade, jalapeño relish, confit potatoes, and coleslaw.

A final note: Many places are seasonal, so check if they’re open if you’re visiting in cooler months.

No more generic resort food. These culinary-savvy properties bring a distinct sense of place to the all-inclusive experience.

#6558. “Schrödinger’s Penguin”: Scientists Discover a Bizarre Paradox Among Endangered Penguins

Endangered erect-crested penguins are holding steady on tiny islands while declining on a breeding ground 40 times larger, challenging assumptions about where the species’ best hope for survival lies.

An endangered penguin species could receive a less severe global risk rating even as one of its only two breeding populations suffers a steep decline. A survey of erect-crested penguins in Aotearoa New Zealand shows how a single assessment of an entire species can conceal very different conservation needs.

The erect-crested penguin is among just four penguin species worldwide listed as “Endangered” on the International Union for Conservation of Nature Red List. Another is New Zealand’s hoiho, or yellow-eyed penguin. Yet while the hoiho has attracted sustained public and conservation attention, the erect-crested penguin remains largely overlooked and is one of the country’s least-studied penguin species.

These birds breed only on the Bounty and Antipodes islands, two remote island groups about 800 kilometers (500 miles) southeast of the South Island. Between 2022 and 2024, researchers used drones to photograph and count every breeding colony across both groups, the first time this had been done for the entire species.

The study, published October 21, 2026, in PLOS ONE, was led by Dr. Thomas Mattern of the Tawaki Project, whose researchers are based in the Departments of Zoology and Marine Science at the University of Otago (Ōtākou Whakaihu Waka). The team collaborated with the Antarctic Research Trust and the Global Penguin Society.

Mattern says, “Comparing the new counts with historical records going back to the mid-1990s, the Bounty Islands population has remained essentially unchanged for at least 25 years.

“The Antipodes Islands population, by contrast, has declined by more than 40 percent since 1995.”

The counts also challenged the historical view of where most of the species breeds.

“The results overturn a long-standing assumption,” Mattern says.

“The tiny Bounty Islands, at just 50 hectares, were found to hold almost as many breeding pairs (about 27,800) as the Antipodes Islands (about 29,800), even though the latter is 40 times larger and historically considered the species’ stronghold.”

The researchers have dubbed the situation “Schrödinger’s Penguin” after the well-known thought experiment in which a cat sealed in a box is imagined to be simultaneously alive and dead until someone opens it and checks. For the penguins, Mattern says, the logic runs in reverse.

“With Schrödinger’s cat, opening the box settles the question one way or the other.

“With Erect-crested penguins, it’s the opposite. From a distance, without proper surveys, everyone assumed there was a single answer for the whole species.

“Once we actually opened the metaphorical box and looked, we found there wasn’t one state at all, but two: stable on the Bounty Islands, declining on the Antipodes Islands.”

On the Antipodes Islands, a shrinking colony may become increasingly difficult for the penguins to defend. Mattern describes how that can compound the losses.

“As Antipodes colonies have shrunk over recent decades, the collective defense they once provided against native subantarctic bird, the skua, a natural predator of eggs and chicks, has weakened, allowing predation losses to increase and colonies to fragment further.”

The islands’ eastern rockhopper penguins had already experienced a population collapse. Their numbers crashed “catastrophically” during the second half of the 20th century, leaving fewer than 1,000 breeding pairs on the Antipodes Islands. The decline mirrored trends elsewhere across the species’ Southern Ocean breeding range and was likely driven by ocean warming.

Co-author Dr. Klemens Pütz of the Antarctic Research Trust suggests that this loss may have changed which penguins the predators targeted.

“As Rockhoppers disappeared, skuas may have turned to Erect-crested penguin eggs and chicks instead,” Pütz says.

Increasingly severe storms, consistent with broader climate trends in the Southern Ocean, have also triggered landslides that break colonies into smaller fragments and put them at further risk. Differences in the birds’ ocean habitats and migration routes likely add to the pressures.

Outside the breeding season, Antipodes birds travel far into the Antarctic Polar Frontal Zone, a region of the Southern Ocean, Mattern says. Bounty Islands birds stay close to their breeding sites in more sheltered waters that may also be more productive.

The contrasting population histories complicate how the species’ extinction risk should be assessed. According to Mattern, its current Endangered ranking rests on inflated population estimates from the 1970s. Reassessing that status against the new data broadly supports the ranking for the Antipodes population, but not for the Bounty population.

“Averaged across both populations, the global ranking would actually improve to “Vulnerable”, masking the severity of the Antipodes decline, and downplaying how exposed the Bounty Islands, likely the species’ last secure stronghold, are to industrial fishing.

“A single, ostensibly improved threat ranking is like putting the lid back on Schrödinger’s box, trading a convenient illusion for the stronger protection the Bounty Islands population actually needs,” Mattern says.

Reference: “Schrödinger’s Penguin? Divergent population trajectories and the challenge of assessing the threat status of the Erect-crested penguin” by Thomas Mattern, Klemens Pütz, Hannah Mattern, Robin Long, Dave Houston, Bianca Keys, Jeff White, Richard Seed, Myrene Otis, Ursula Ellenberg, Pablo Garcia-Borboroglu and Benno Lüthi, 21 October 2026, PLOS ONE. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0359075

The study was funded by the Vontobel Foundation (Switzerland) through the Antarctic Research Trust, the Global Penguin Society, and conducted under permits from the New Zealand Department of Conservation.

#6557. Game Theory Helps SETI Search for Alien Civilizations

The Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI) is mostly concerned with where to look for technosignatures from another civilization. Between 2012 and 2015, SETI's Project Phoenix targeted about 1,000 Sun-like stars for signs of Intelligent life. But where to look might not be as important as when to look, according to scientists at SETI.

In a new paper, scientists outline the effort to search for signals not only in the right place, but at the right time. The paper is "A Technosignature Survey Of The Anti-Solar Point: The SETI Institute's Largest-Ever Campaign With The Allen Telescope Array," and it was presented at the 77th International Astronautical Congress. The authors are Isabel Gerrard and Sofia Z. Sheikh. Gerrard is the Technosignature Researcher with Breakthrough Listen at the University of Oxford, and Sheikh is a SETI Institute Research Scientist.

âThe challenge in SETI isnât simply deciding where to point a telescope. Itâs figuring out where and when another civilization might choose to transmit." - Dr. Sofia Sheikh, SETI Institute Research Scientist.

The new search effort doesn't do away with the "where" aspect of the search. Since life exists around stars, this search is still focused on stars, or rather the planets that orbit them. But it's different this time. This time it involves a point changes over time, called the antisolar point. It's the point in space-time that's directly opposite from the Sun from the perspective of an observer.

Imagine a line extending from the Sun, through an observer on Earth, and out the other side. It's not fixed in place; it's an abstract point defined by changing coordinates that shifts as the Earth orbits the Sun.

This simple static illustration shows the antisolar point. (created with AI)

This new SETI effort is also inspired by game theory. Game theory is a way of anticipating another player's moves in a game, when their moves are also based on their anticipations of your next move. The most well-known example of game theory is probably the Prisoner's Dilemma. In this case, the other player is another intelligent civilization conducting their own SETI-like effort.

What it boils down to is trying to predict when and where we can detect a purposeful transmission from another civilization and send our own, and also when and where they're doing the same.

"We borrow from game theory the concept of Schelling points to hypothesize spacetime coordinates where both we and an extraterrestrial agent might send and search for a signal," the authors write. Schelling points are also called focal points in game theory. "From the perspective opposite the Sun, an extraterrestrial agent could detect Earth transiting within the habitable zone, thus this Anti-Solar Point (ASP) poses a shared and salient Schelling point."

Resources are limited, and the better we or an alien civilization can use them, the greater the chances of success. If they can figure out the most effective time and place to send a radio signal, they increase their chances of success. The same is true for us. There's a synergy in it.

"A Schelling point is a default solution two agents both naturally arrive at, without communication, because of some shared cultural understanding of prominence in the given context," the authors write. "The predictability of a Schelling point relies on a common understanding of the prominent features in this context, and the mutual awareness of each otherâs knowledge."

So without any prior communication, both we and another extraterrestrial agent would identify the same place to send and receive signals: the antisolar point. The choice is based on our shared understanding of astronomical transits, or what we call the transit method in the hunt for exoplanets. It's almost certain that another civilization would also use this method because it presents itself naturally.

"It follows that if an ETA (Extraterrestrial Agent) also used the transit method in their search for life, they would detect Earth against the Sun as habitable and classify Earth as an eligible target for interstellar communication," the researchers explain.

This simple animation shows how the antisolar point moves and how an exterrestrial observer would detect Earth's transit. (AI-generated)

At the midpoint of Earth's transit in front of the Sun, from the ETA's perspective, Earth would be directly between them and the Sun. "From the perspective opposite the Sun, once each year an extraterrestrial agent could detect Earth transiting within the habitable zone, thus this antisolar point poses a shared and salient time-coordinate Schelling point," the authors write.

The search using the Allen Telescope Array and the antisolar point is called the ATA-ASP survey. It's a multiyear effort, and its initial findings are already here. Because it's based on the ASP, the survey isn't constant, it's intermittent. As Earth orbits the Sun, the ASP keeps changing, and it takes several years to cover it.

One of the Allen Telescope Array's dishes. The ATA-ASP survey will be the ATA's largest survey effort, collecting 11 petabytes of data over four years. Image Credit: Photo taken by Isabel Gerrard and edited by Ananya Kalapatapu

"Provided that half of the ecliptic is inaccessible in a year (the portion that is daytime), the campaign requires at least two years of observing sessions to sample every possible ASP along the ecliptic," the authors explain. "Furthermore, due to the â¼ 365.25 day orbit of the Earth (inciting the leap day every 4 years), the accessible nighttime portion of the ecliptic slightly precesses in successive years, ergo total survey coverage requires staggering observations over the course of four years." For these reasons, the ATA isn't solely occupied with the ATA-ASP survey.

The first pilot results are from August August 30th, 2024 until August 25th, 2026. Obviously, ATA-ASP didn't detect any alien signals or we would've almost certainly heard about them already. But for SETI, the results mark a milestone. Searching the ASP for signals was first proposed decades ago, and now they've finally done it.

ATA-ASP detected an enormous number of radio signals, about 1.9 million in 17 hours of observations. But they were all from human sources. Those detections were still an important test of the system though.

As things stand now, the ATA-ASP campaign has gathered another 121 nights of observations since the initial pilot. Those results haven't been shared yet.

âThe challenge in SETI isnât simply deciding where to point a telescope,â said co-author Sheikh. âItâs figuring out where and when another civilization might choose to transmit. The anti-solar point gives us a way to think about that problem from the perspective of a potential sender, rather than just the receiver.â
