#6488. This Snapmaker 3D Printer Makes Multicolor Prints Faster—and Wastes Less Filament

Affordable, efficient multi-toolhead printing brings your prints to life.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The Snapmaker U1 revolutionized multi-material 3D printing when it launched in late 2025, introducing a clever toolhead swapping system that speeds up the process of switching between colors or materials, while minimizing the waste it normally generates.

Most 3D printers use a single nozzle to lay down layers of plastic, but the U1 features a set of four nozzles, each of which pulls from its own filament feed. When it’s time to change color or material, the printer swaps the entire toolhead automatically, which takes about five seconds—up to four times faster than most single-head printers can change colors. The mere concept garnered record-setting support in the U1’s pre-release Kickstarter campaign. It helped that, at $750, it was far more affordable than any other multihead printer.

And, upon testing, it turns out that the printer is everything Snapmaker’s supporters hoped it would be. I added the U1 to our guide to 3D printers earlier this year based on some initial testing, but have now had it in my lab for about a year.

The multihead system is indeed faster and more efficient, and U1’s user interface makes it a genuine pleasure to use. Since my initial testing, a new technology called “full spectrum printing” has come out that greatly expands the options for multicolor printing, especially for multi-toolhead printers like the U1.

All of that only reaffirms the U1’s place among my favorite printers right now: It’s an easy recommendation for anyone looking to upgrade or even get their start with 3D printing, especially if you plan on making multicolor or mixed-media prints.

The Snapmaker U1 is a CoreXY printer, which means that the print heads move left and right and forward and back, while the bed moves up and down. (As opposed to a “bed-slinger” that moves the print bed forward and back, while the print head moves up and down.) The toolheads are held on a rack at the back of the print chamber, and all four sides have windows, which makes it easy to visually monitor your prints.

It produces crisp, detailed prints with minimal fuss. Between my initial testing and recent revisit, I logged over 165 hours of print time, creating models of all shapes and sizes, from small, intricately detailed miniatures to large vases and accessories for my table saw and shop vacuum.

Snapmaker provides a free, reskinned version of Orca—a popular “slicer” program that breaks down 3D models into layer-based blueprints for printing. It’s also compatible with any slicer software you prefer. I had issues with the speed of Snapmaker’s slicer when I first tested the U1 last year, but I’m happy to report that the latest versions of the software run more smoothly.

The model I tested did not have a top lid. This is fine for filaments with lower print temperatures, such as PLA (polylactide), but can be an issue if you want the more durable prints that require higher temperature or foul-smelling filaments. Snapmaker currently offers an add-on lid and HEPA/activated carbon air filter for $150, allowing you to have more control over the internal temperature of the chamber, and to control fumes from printing. But even with the lid, the Snapmaker U1 has no active chamber heater—it relies on the heat from the nozzle and bed to maintain the chamber temperature. This means printing high-temperature filaments like ASA (acrylonitrile styrene acrylate) or ABS (acrylonitrile butadiene styrene) can be difficult. (If this is an issue for you, consider our Best for Durable Prints pick, the Bambu X2D.)

The defining characteristic of the U1 is its four separate toolheads, and its efficiency during multicolor or multimaterial prints. A 3D printer with a single toolhead can create multicolor prints, but it’s a laborious process. To switch colors, the printer needs to clip the current filament, purge any excess material from the nozzle, then feed in the next filament. And it will go through that full process on every single color switch. A complex print may have several hundred filament changes, which will add long stretches of inactivity, as well as mounds and mounds of waste. That’s why it pays to spring for a multi-toolhead printer. They can swap among a limited number of colors without changing filaments, minimizing time and material losses.

To demonstrate the difference, I printed the left and right cheeks of a mask on the Snapmaker U1 and the Bambu P2S, our current Best Overall printer. (The models were identical, only mirrored to more easily tell one from the other.) While the P2S excels at standalone printing, the difference in print material and time is staggering.

Even in a small, hand-sized print, it makes a huge difference. On a larger or more complex job, you could save a meaningful amount of money (by keeping your filament on the spool).

That efficiency when swapping colors makes the Snapmaker U1 particularly well-suited for one of the newest developments in multicolor printing: Full spectrum printing, which allows the printer to blend filament colors by laying down thin, semi-translucent layers of filament on top of each other to create a wider array of colors, much like an ink-jet printer.

Traditionally, 3D printers cannot create or control color: The color (or colors) of your materials are your only options, and you need to have spools of filament for every color you want to use. Even with four printer heads, that can be fairly limiting. After years of using 3D printers and dealing with all the labor and waste around switching colors, the ability to blend colors feels shocking in the best way possible. It’s absolutely liberating.

Since full spectrum printing was developed as an open-source technique, it isn’t exclusive to the U1; but it was developed with this printer in mind. And the full spectrum technique of applying many thin layers of filament means that it’s ideal for use with a multi-toolhead printer like the U1. Snapmaker’s slicer fully integrates full spectrum printing, meaning that you can begin using it at no cost.

It’s worth noting, though, that other manufacturers are hot on Snapmaker’s tail, releasing their own tool-changing printers and embracing full spectrum technology. But, for now at least, full spectrum printing makes the U1 a wonderfully distinctive choice, capable of doing a lot of things that most other 3D printers can’t. (At least not without wasting a metric ton of filament).

Of course, all the technical bells and whistles don’t mean a thing if the printer itself is so difficult to use that it sits idle. Luckily, the U1 has a user-friendly design that frees you up to focus on making things, rather than endlessly tweaking poorly labeled settings, or scouring the internet for solutions to what should be a simple issue.

The U1 is more intuitive than most printers, and that’s clear right from the moment you unpack the machine. The U1 comes with an extensive, step-by-step assembly document, with full-color images of each step and a QR code that links to a video walkthrough. I loved that it shipped with extra parts, so a broken part doesn’t bring you to a complete standstill until you order a replacement. And the U1 comes with a generous amount of starter filament, with 500 grams of four colors, compared to most printers that ship with only a few grams, enough for no more than a single test print.

I rarely ran into print issues, but when I did, the AI detection worked well, pausing prints and allowing me to clear debris or cancel the job without wasting more filament.

One of the previous drawbacks of the Snapmaker U1 ecosystem at launch was that it lacked an online model repository. There are plenty of online communities that have grown up around the U1, such as on Facebook and Reddit, but model-sharing spaces serve as both a repository of knowledge and a way to find 3D designs built specifically for your machine, keeping tinkering to a minimum.

Happily, the brand has finally addressed this, launching Snapmaker Space, which is currently in open beta. If you buy this printer, it’s definitely worth checking out. It doesn’t have a community section yet, and I’m hopeful it will be added soon. After all, areas where makers can share ideas and test designs are exactly what creates innovation.

Given its four-headed design and some innovative software, the Snapmaker U1 is my go-to recommendation for anyone who wants a user-friendly option to regularly print multiple colors or materials. The U1 is beautifully designed and the user interface is a genuine pleasure to use, and its combination of performance and quality design makes it a great choice for a majority of users. Its competitors are more expensive or more difficult to use, making the U1 the natural choice for makers who want a balance of price and multicolor performance.

There are exceptions, of course. For example, a printer like the Creality K2 Pro Combo makes more sense if you’re planning to work with engineering-grade filaments like PC (polycarbonate) or ASA (acrylonitrile styrene acrylate), since you’ll need a filtered ventilation system and the higher temperatures that come with active chamber heating. (Though that will also push the retail price up more than $1,000.) On the other hand, at $750, the Snapmaker U1 may be a bit pricey for new makers: If you’re on a tighter budget, I’d recommend looking at options like the Elegoo Centauri Carbon, a single-head printer that starts at less than $300, and features a multicolor add-on.

Still, the U1 is a stellar all-around pick that delivers great performance, especially if you’re working with multiple colors. After a year, it has become one of my go-to printers across the board. Whether you’re printing a cute multicolor fidget spinner for your kids or assembling prototypes to impress investors, this is a printer capable of turning your vision into reality.

A former residential remodeler and maintenance manager, Dan Stout has worked in nearly every part of the construction and DIY industry, from project planning and permitting to plumbing, drywall, carpentry, and more. He loves to write about the weird history of everyday objects, and to help readers make informed decisions about their homes.

#6487. Chemical Breakthrough Could Unlock the “Holy Grail” of Solid-State Battery Technology

Scientists in China have developed a thin protective coating that could help overcome a major obstacle to longer-lasting, high-capacity batteries. In laboratory tests, solid-state batteries using the treated lithium metal retained 82.3% of their initial capacity after 300 charging cycles, compared with just 43.0% for batteries using untreated lithium.

The researchers at Xidian University developed a simple liquid coating that reacts with lithium metal to form a protective barrier. Their findings, published in Science China Chemistry, suggest a possible route toward safer, more durable batteries for electric vehicles and energy storage.

Lithium metal has been called the “holy grail” of energy storage because it can theoretically store nearly ten times as much charge per gram as the graphite used in conventional lithium-ion batteries. Its exceptional capacity could enable lighter batteries that store more energy and potentially support longer driving ranges.

To address this problem, researchers led by Professors Siwu Li, Weiwei Wu, and Chuang Yu combined a silicon-based polymer with indium chloride. When applied to lithium, the mixture forms lithium fluoride and lithium-indium alloy nanoparticles within a flexible protective film just 12 micrometers thick (about 0.00047 inches).

“This hybrid layer acts like a smart fortress,” explains corresponding author Siwu Li. “The polymer backbone provides flexibility to absorb the mechanical stress of lithium expanding and contracting. The lithium fluoride phase blocks electrons to prevent dendrite nucleation. And the lithium-indium alloy nanoparticles act as traffic conductors, guiding lithium ions to deposit evenly rather than piling up in dangerous spikes.”

The coated lithium electrodes withstood a critical current density of 3.5 milliamperes per square centimeter, more than four times the 0.8 achieved by untreated lithium. In complete batteries containing a nickel-cobalt-manganese oxide cathode and a sulfide solid electrolyte, the protected electrodes delivered an initial capacity of 129.8 milliampere-hours per gram and retained 82.3% after 300 cycles at 0.5C.

Spectroscopy and electron microscopy confirmed the coating’s composition and revealed a dense, uniform layer without visible cracks or gaps.

The coating could help address the chemical instability between lithium metal and sulfide solid electrolytes, a major challenge in solid-state battery development.

Because the protective layer forms from an applied liquid, it may be compatible with existing industrial coating equipment without requiring expensive vacuum processing. The researchers also plan to explore alternatives to indium, including tin and zinc.

Although commercial performance remains unproven, the findings offer a promising approach to making high-energy lithium metal batteries more stable and longer-lasting.

Reference: “In situ reductive construction of a silicon-based polymer/indium alloy hybrid layer for stable lithium metal anodes in sulfide solid-state batteries” by Kun Song, Qun Zhao, Xianbo Zhao, Siwu Li, Jun Liu, Haitao Chen, Weiwei Wu and Chuang Yu, 6 August 2026, Science China Chemistry. DOI: 10.1007/s11426-026-3450-y

#6486. It’s Almost a Year Since the FCC Banned Most New Consumer Drones: We Rank the Ones Still on Sale

Almost no new drones launched in the U.S. in 2026. These are the best old models still flying (and on sale) from brands we trust.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The FCC’s decision to ban the import of foreign-made drones last December effectively ground the entire category to a halt. Only a handful of new drones hit stores this year, mostly because they received approval prior to the ban, so the options we have when we need a new one have stayed more or less the same since then. Outside the U.S., companies like DJI are still putting out new drones: As they move on to bigger and better, we can’t help but wonder if or when we’ll start to see supplies of U.S.-approved models dry up.

So far, things seem pretty stable. Many of our favorites remain available, and there are a few we’re still hoping to test. We’re hoping that some domestic brands pick up the slack and start innovating in the field, but, for now, we’ve decided to keep a running “still-fly” list of the ones you can still buy in case supplies start to thin out.

To be clear, this isn’t a comprehensive list of every possible available drone. (Frankly, that wouldn’t be helpful. Not every drone is worth monitoring.) Instead, think of it as merely a long list of drones, both tested and untested, that we’re keeping an eye on as viable options in case our top recommendations go out of stock. I’ve also ranked these options, roughly, based on their core specs, including camera quality, battery power, range, and price.

DJI’s U.S.-available flagship drone, the Mavic 4 Pro, offers perhaps the best camera capabilities and clarity of footage of any consumer-grade drone out there right now. It has three distinct cameras: a 28mm lens for crisp details and low-light shooting, a 70mm medium tele lens for portraits and medium-range shooting, and a 168mm tele lens for long-range shooting. They operate on a 360-degree gimbal, so you have full control to record stills and video up close or from a distance, and at any angle.

Beyond the cameras, the drone comes with a powerful motor and long-lasting battery that allows you to fly in windy conditions and still come home with stable, clear footage. We don’t expect the average person to need three high-resolution cameras, 51 minutes of battery, and a top speed of 50 mph, but if you’re more than a hobby flyer, it’s hard to find a better choice.

One of the most affordable and easy-to-fly drones from DJI, the original DJI Neo is an older model that’s perfect for a beginner who wants to learn the ropes. The caged propellers are very helpful to pilots who lack a certain level of nuance with the controls and are prone to crashing. The cage prevents damage to the propellers or the motor.

At the same time, in our own testing, the Neo was exceptionally easy to steer with smooth, responsive controls and several preset flight modes that fly the drone automatically in specific patterns. While you can’t expect professional-grade footage, the 4K camera will be more than enough for casual fliers.

I’ve rated this drone so highly because the price tag is so low. There is a newer version, the Neo 2, with better specs, and normally I’d recommend going with the newer model to reduce the chances that DJI might stop supporting the Neo with security updates. Given the circumstances, though, future-proofing is less of a factor here. And it’s very hard to pass up a drone of this quality at such a low price.

The Autel Evo II is a thermal imaging drone, primarily designed for search and rescue operations, power plant inspections, and even to assist firefighters. In theory, it could also be a useful tool for hunters looking to identify wildlife from a distance. Its thermal imaging camera can detect a subject from up to 100 meters away, even if they’re visually obscured by brush or obstacles.

It’s also quite powerful: The Evo II can fly up to 45 mph, so it can reach the edge of its nine-mile range in just 12 minutes. With 16x zoom, it can also scan nearby areas for small thermal signatures with relative ease.

Between its specific use case and very high price tag, this is not a drone for the average person. But it should be very capable in the right hands.

Like the DJI Neo, the HoverAir X1 is a small camera drone that’s both durable and fairly affordable, which makes it a great choice for beginners. The biggest difference is that the X1 is made for truly novice pilots who don’t trust their skills at all.

While you can fly it manually, the drone comes loaded with a number of preprogrammed flight patterns and flying modes that don’t require any piloting at all. The auto-follow feature allows you to essentially launch and forget about it. At a top speed of around 15 miles per hour, you can bike or even snowboard with the drone to capture footage.

At the same time, the propellers are protected by the wraparound frame made of a flexible polymer. So, in the case of a crash, no harm, no foul. I personally love the foldable design. Folded down, I’m able to fit the entire drone in my pocket.

The drone we recommend for most people, regardless of experience or use case, DJI Mini 4K, is a decently affordable jack-of-all-trades.

For $300, the Mini 4K has a ton of great features that empower both new and veteran users, including pre-programmed routes, one-touch takeoff, and an automatic return-to-home system. The GPS-enabled return home system is a popular feature on many drones but one not common on a model in this price range.

That said, the Mini is more than a mere fly-toy. It features a 4K camera and level 5 wind resistance, allowing it to handle in gusts up to 24 miles per hour so you can film on gusty days. The battery life is short, but functional: With the three batteries you get in this set, you should get over 90 minutes of flight time, so it’s set for leisurely flight or most short-term survey and recording tasks.

There aren’t many drone brands with a reputation for making reliable “prosumer” drones that deliver the kind of build quality and performance you want for serious projects at a price hobbyists can afford. As a result, DJI has become a singularly dominant brand, but there are brands like Potensic out there cultivating a similar track record, even if their footprints are smaller.

The Atom SE is another great starter, given the price and solid maneuverability. It’s a very solid drone with a lot of cool features and few significant downsides. It can fly continuously for over 30 minutes on a full charge, films in 4K, and has a few programmable flight modes for hands-free flying.

Another unique feature is the GPS auto return: No matter where you are, you can press a button and the drone will begin flying to you. This particular SE kit comes with a controller that is compatible with your smartphone for integrated flying and real-time footage.

With a more powerful motor and a greater selection of preprogrammed flight patterns than the classic X1, the X1 Promax is a definite upgrade on the classic X1 for folks looking for a bit more power and a wider array of features, even as they’re still getting the hang of drone control.

Much like the X1, the Promax is both supremely portable and durable. The protective cage around the propellers means it can take a ton of pretty hefty crashes without causing any serious damage. At the same time, it has the same foldable build so it fits perfectly in a pocket. That makes it an awesome action cam alternative for outdoor adventurers who want a remote cameraman to help film extreme sports like snowboarding or dirt biking.

Like the X1 Promax, the Potensic Atom 2 drone offers a more feature-rich (and expensive) step up from the brand’s basic Atom SE. The drone has an incredibly clear 4K camera, over 30 minutes of flight time, and a pretty impressive top speed of close to 36 mph. In comparison to the SE, the Atom 2 makes some notable improvements. These include filming at a higher frame rate, offering more than double the range, providing a three-axis gimbal for greater video stability, and including AI digital tracking for better hands-free flying.

During testing, I was really impressed by how responsive it feels in the air. I was a novice pilot when I used it, but was able to fly it with more finesse and nuance than many of the drones I’d tried before, including some more expensive models. And it’s easy to fly the Atom 2 by pairing it with your phone, though the kit I’ve highlighted here comes with a dedicated controller with a large view screen.

If you want clearer, cleaner footage and a bit more power from your motor, this is your answer over the Atom SE.

The DJI Neo 2 is another upgraded riff on a core favorite of mine, with some notable upgrades and a substantially higher price tag. Unsurprisingly, this upgraded model features upgraded performance across the board, including stronger wind resistance, faster tracking speed, and two-axis stability for smoother video while hovering or flying. It’s also still quite durable, with enclosed propellers that provide extra protection against crashes that might otherwise cause damage to delicate parts of the drone.

The Atom 3 is Potensic’s newest drone, and the brand’s flagship model. Its best quality is its tremendous battery life, up to 50 minutes of continuous flight on a single charge. The camera also gets an upgrade, with a three-axis gimbal for more control and better stability while shooting on the move, even in high winds.

It also boasts a solid top speed of 36 mph, a 4K camera with an AI-enhanced night mode for better clarity during night shoots, and a nearly 10-mile range, which is notably larger than both the Atom SE and Atom 2.

The improvements on the Atom 3 won’t be huge for the average flier, but could definitely make a difference for those shooting serious footage or who want to fly for a lot longer before swapping batteries. If the Atom SE is for the new pilots, and the Atom 2 is for moderate hobbyists looking for a premium camera, then the Atom 3 is a serious upgrade for expert pilots who need both precision flight control and a prosumer-grade camera.

Easily the most notable new drone of 2026, the Antigravity A1 is a high-end camera drone built for speed and aerial acrobatics. The controls include a pair of viewfinder goggles that give you the full UAV pilot experience, which should make for more thrilling flights. (And more precise recording if you’re using it for creative work.) Meanwhile, the hand controls blend conventional button inputs with motion controls for smooth turns and nuanced, intuitive flight control.

Candidly, I haven’t tested the A1 yet, but I’m hoping to soon. It’s an interesting and exciting take that represents everything we’d like to see when and if the drone market restabilizes.

Holy Stone isn’t as well known as many of the other brands on this list. The brand makes affordable drones with functional controls and solid design. The HS360E isn’t quite as impressive as DJI’s Mini or the HoverAir X1 on paper, but you’re still getting a 4K camera drone with some premium features at a very reasonable price.

Another drone that lets you see through the camera using display goggles, the DJI Avata 2 is ideal for acrobatic flying and high-speed video on a bit more of a budget. The goggles offer real-time POV footage of what your drone sees while the one-handed control works using the motion of your wrist to turn or accelerate.

What sets this drone apart from most others is how capable it is of genuinely acrobatic flight. It can flip, roll, or even drift 180 degrees with ease, so you can pilot it hard and with intention without fear of going beyond its means.

With a close-to-45-minute flight time and both medium- and wide-angle cameras, this is a great drone for long filming sessions over landscapes. In fact, the drone even comes with 45 gigabytes of internal storage so you can save tons of footage directly to the device without worrying about uploading it to a cloud-based storage system.

The Air 3S also has omnidirectional obstacle sensing so it will make adjustments to avoid crashing into walls or trees even when flying at high speeds.

I wouldn’t expect this drone to win in a race, but a bubble drone seems like a pretty good time if you’ve got young kids, and it’s the only one I’ve seen from a notable brand with this kind of a feature. The HS320 bubble drone is built with an internal bubble machine that sprays hundreds of bubbles as it flies over you.

Notably, this drone does not feature a camera. That it’s more of a toy than a tool works in its favor, I think, because that keeps the price down. At under $100, this is a great way to liven up an afternoon in the backyard, but also a really easy entry point for folks who want to learn how to fly.

#6485. Scientists Find a Clever Way to Read Quantum Information Without Destroying It

Simulations suggest that one type of qubit could reveal its state through its own electric current, helping researchers monitor quantum computers with less disturbance and fewer components.

Like a bit in an ordinary computer, a qubit stores information using states labeled 0 and 1. A qubit can also be prepared in a superposition, a quantum combination of the two. These states belong to a physical system that researchers build and control. In the design explored here, that system is a tiny wire connected to superconducting materials.

The aim of quantum computing is to use quantum behavior to perform certain calculations more efficiently than conventional computers. That requires control: researchers must prepare qubits and change their states deliberately. Unwanted interactions with the surroundings can disrupt them, and measuring a qubit can alter it, too.

A theoretical study proposes reading one type of qubit through an electric current it produces itself. This could let researchers follow its behavior with minimal disturbance and without the extra qubits used in many existing methods.

Andreev qubits hold information in states formed between superconducting materials, which carry electric current without resistance. They are named after Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939–2023), who described the underlying process at the boundary between normal and superconducting materials in 1964.

“In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot—that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined – formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It’s in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed,” explains José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil.

“In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained,” says Egues.

Many existing methods use a helper quantum system called an ancilla. Researchers prepare it, connect it to the qubit, transfer information to it, and measure it to preserve the original qubit as much as possible. These steps add time and equipment. “Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself,” says Egues.

The qubit would sit in a closed superconducting circuit carrying a supercurrent, an electric current that flows without resistance. The calculations predict that interference between the states in the qubit’s superposition makes part of this current oscillate. “It’s precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It’s that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal,” Egues points out.

An applied voltage usually causes this kind of oscillation, known as the AC Josephson effect. “Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It’s the very evolution of the qubit’s state that produces that oscillation,” says Egues.

A nearby superconducting quantum interference device, or SQUID, would act as the detector. These instruments are extremely sensitive to weak magnetic fields. Egues explains, “We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID ‘senses’ that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small.”

Identifying the qubit’s state requires knowing both the balance of 0 and 1 and their relative phase, or how the two components line up.

“Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it’s possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit,” Egues explains.

Researchers could also track the qubit through repeated readings without resetting it to its initial state after each measurement.

Simulations included measurement noise and feedback from the small detection coil. They indicated that the detector’s influence could become negligible, with readout accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%, depending on the number of measurements. These values fall within standard thresholds adopted in quantum error correction schemes.

“Our method doesn’t eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits – the ancillas – employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols,” Egues notes.

The work, published in Physical Review B Letters, was led by Egues and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. SQUID detection of extremely small currents and magnetic fields is already established, and Egues says the proposal would not require future advances in materials or device fabrication.

“All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn’t yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed,” he argues.

Reference: “Andreev qubit readout from dynamic interference supercurrent” by Xian-Peng Zhang, Chuanchang Zeng, Zhen-Biao Yang, Jose Carlos Egues and Yugui Yao, 5 August 2026, Physical Review B. DOI: 10.1103/6gkt-hghj

The best time to see meteors during the Southern Taurid meteor shower is coming up soon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of autumn's best opportunities to see brilliant "fireballs" arrives overnight Wednesday and Thursday (Nov. 4-5) during the Southern Taurid meteor shower.

Although the Southern Taurids are a minor meteor shower that produces only a handful of "shooting stars" each hour, it occasionally features exceptionally bright meteors called fireballs, which can briefly light up the night sky. According to NASA, fireballs are meteors at least as bright as Venus.

The Southern Taurids are active for several weeks in fall and peak Oct. 14, but the American Meteor Society expects the "fireball swarm component" to peak around Nov. 4-5.

Meteors can streak across any part of the sky, but for this meteor shower, they appear to radiate from the constellation Taurus, which will rise in the eastern sky as night falls and climb higher as the night progresses. That makes the hours around midnight a good time to look for shooting stars. However, unlike major meteor showers such as the Perseids (which peak Aug. 12-13) and the Geminids (which peak Dec. 13-14), the Southern Taurids have a broad peak, so there's no need to be outside at an exact time.

The Southern Taurids are the first of two fireball-rich meteor showers to be visible this month. The Northern Taurids will peak overnight on Nov. 11-12, giving stargazers another chance to spot a fireball. Both meteor showers result from dust and debris left in the inner solar system by Comet 2P/Encke striking Earth's atmosphere.

Discovered in 1786, Encke is a massive comet, measuring 2.98 miles (4.8 kilometers) in diameter, according to NASA ‪—‬ around one-third the size of the object thought to have killed the nonavian dinosaurs. Encke orbits the sun every 3.3 years, one of the shortest known orbital periods of any comet in the solar system. Scientists theorize that Encke is one of many fragments of a giant comet that broke apart 20,000 to 30,000 years ago.

After the Southern and Northern Taurids, the next meteor shower will be the Leonids, which peak Nov. 17-18 and produce around 15 shooting stars per hour, and the Geminids, which peak Dec. 13-14 and can deliver up to 120 shooting stars per hour close to the peak.

It's best to watch meteor showers with the naked eye, but a good backyard telescope will serve you well in the months to come. As the long nights of winter kick off in the Northern Hemisphere, skywatching opportunities abound — including four consecutive supermoons from Nov. 2026 to Feb. 2027.

#6483. Some of the world’s biggest bats are getting smaller

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Madagascan flying foxes, easy targets for hunters, have shrunk since the 1980s

Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus) (shown) have skulls that are 6 percent smaller than they were prior to the 1980s. Large-scale hunting by humans may be the reason.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

These big bats aren’t quite the behemoths they used to be.

With a leathery wingspan of up to a meter and a half, fruit bats —some of which are called flying foxes — feel a bit like they’ve flapped out of a fantasy novel. Though flying foxes include the world’s largest bats, one species in Madagascar appears to be shrinking, researchers report October 29 in the Journal of Mammalogy. Hunting pressure by humans may be why.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The first hints that the bats might be shrinking came from scientific collections at the Field Museum in Chicago. Researchers at the museum — including flying vertebrate ecologist Emily Cornelius Ruhs and conservation biologist Steven Goodman — noticed something strange about the preserved specimens of Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus).

“It seemed like the [flying foxes] in the collections were a lot larger than the ones that [field scientists] had been catching in recent years in Madagascar,” says Ruhs.

To see if newer specimens were indeed smaller than older specimens, and to understand why, the researchers began taking detailed measurements of the bats. The team logged measurements of 12 different features of the skull and teeth over a total of 121 specimens stored within nine museums. The specimens were collected over more than 150 years, up to the present day.

Bats collected prior to the 1980s had skulls that were on average 3.6 millimeters longer, or about 6 percent longer, than those collected after the 1980s. Possible causes of the shrinkage included effects from climate change or habitat loss. But the timing of the shrinkage also lined up with the commercialization of flying fox hunting.

“Bats are eaten in Madagascar in certain villages and cultures,” Ruhs says. Up until the 1980s, the animals were mostly hunted on a very small scale to provide food for a family or small community. But around that time, people started selling more bats at markets and restaurants.

As hunting pressure increased, the biggest bats in the population may have been selectively targeted since they provide the “most bang for your buck” Ruhs says.

It’s possible that the smaller size could have long-term impacts on the population, says Emma Stone, a conservation biologist at the University of Bath in England. “Species are specifically adapted to their environments and adaptation takes place over thousands of years,” she says. Changes in the animals’ physical traits or adaptations caused by human pressures might make the bats less able to respond to environmental, climate or disease stresses.

The bats’ population has dwindled as well. There were an estimated 300,000 Malagasy flying foxes in Madagascar in the early 2000s. Researchers estimate the number has dropped two-thirds since then. The new findings raise concerns about how the bats’ shrinking bodies might be a bellwether for species-wide conservation risks. Future work on the bats’ genetics could tell researchers how modern populations are faring, Ruhs says. Other fruit bat species are also hunted and eaten in Madagascar, she notes, so seeing if similar shrinkage is happening in those species might be interesting.

“These are important food sources for people. But I think there is something to be said for understanding how to manage [their harvesting] a little bit more,” Ruhs says. “If this population isn’t doing so well, how do we overcome the needs of the people who live there while also protecting species?”

This story was updated on October 29, 2026 to include expert input from Emma Stone.

#6482. The Weber Genesis Costs Twice as Much as My Spirit Grill—and It’s Worth It

More space, faster heat, and better storage make this Weber worth the splurge.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Grilling has gotten me outside more than any other activity in the past two years, and—not to brag—I run a lot. Between hosting friends on any given three-day weekend, holiday parties, and weeknight dinners, I use my grill as much as possible. Weber’s Spirit grill was the gateway to this newfound personality trait. It evangelized me to propane grilling and outdoor cooking in general (my Recteq smoker deserves equal praise).

Growing up, my dad refused to cook on a gas grill, but I found charcoal time-consuming and messy as hell. My Spirit lights up fast, is easy to maintain, and was the perfect start to entrench me in the grilling lifestyle. However, nothing gold can stay, and I needed (ok, wanted) an upgrade.

Weber’s Genesis grills were the heir apparent. The range offers more storage, more power from each burner, and better overall build quality. On paper, it’s a clear upgrade from the brand’s Spirit line, but how does that translate in person? I found out it’s a well-worth-it upgrade that elevates my grilling experience.

I love Weber, but I admit the names can be a bit complicated. At least the naming system is consistent across the brand, as I ran into the same thing when shopping Spirit grills. The letters and numbers describe the materials used, the number of burners, and each grill's features. Here’s a quick and easy breakdown:

My Spirit grill was an E-210, and my Genesis is an E-330. The obvious difference is the extra burner on the Genesis, but both are base models in their respective lineups, making them easier to compare.

Improved build quality is a tricky thing to discern from a product listing. It’s subjective, since people define quality differently, but in my opinion, the Genesis is indeed improved. It feels much more substantial than the Spirit in hand, with sturdy metal hardware, and I immediately noticed the difference when I separated the parts and hardware for the Genesis. There’s a lot less plastic, and everything feels secure.

The Genesis also has a cleaner design, which makes storage more efficient. An extra side cabinet stores grates and accessories, and the propane cabinet has room for even more. Four locking caster wheels prop the grill and propane tank up off the ground. On the Spirit, the propane tank sits on the ground, making it hard to move.

Two side tables provide plenty of prep space and don’t fold down as they do on the Spirit. They can be swapped out for Weber Works accessories, letting me reconfigure the grill to my cooking needs.

Grills are aesthetically pleasing to me as is, but even more so when it comes to Weber’s Stealth Edition grills. They feature an all-black design with a matte black lid, black trim, side tables, handles, knobs, wheels, and a separate sear burner controlled by a metallic red knob. The Stealth Edition costs about $200 extra, so it's up to you whether it’s worth it.

Going from two burners to three burners inevitably adds cooking space, but I didn’t expect to love it this much. I went from 450 square inches of primary cooking space (not including the top rack) on the Spirit to 513 square inches on the Genesis. Only 73 inches more, but it feels so much bigger in action, and I no longer need to cook in batches for large groups.

The extra burner also means it heats up much faster than my old grill. When searing Force of Nature and Snake River Farms NY strip and ribeyes, I got the grill up to 500 degrees Fahrenheit in about two and a half minutes. All that extra firepower also makes the warming rack a bona fide cooking space on its own. I grilled burgers on the primary space while fully cooking hot dogs on the warming rack over Labor Day weekend.

The Genesis grates can also be flipped and reconfigured with Weber Crafted accessories. This lets you expand cooking methods and upgrade grates and cookware later, so you don’t get bored with your setup.

I’ll always have a place in my heart for my Spirit grill. It’s small, efficient, and saw me through many block parties and gatherings, but it was time for a change. The Weber Genesis E-330 is the perfect mid-range upgrade I was looking for—more space, more firepower, and more storage. All of these features have improved my grilling experience and made it markedly more enjoyable. I realize the price difference is nothing to scoff at; $500 isn’t chump change, but it’s worth the splurge if you know you want to grill often

#6481. A Hidden Substance in Drinking Water May Be Linked to Heart Problems in Children

The water we drink may hold clues to a rare heart condition in children, but whether naturally occurring lithium plays a role in its development remains unknown.

A dangerously fast heartbeat can begin with an extra strand of heart muscle that forms before birth. The strand creates an abnormal electrical connection, allowing the heart’s rhythm to go awry. Doctors can eliminate these connections, but a larger question has remained largely unanswered. Why do they develop in the first place?

A study led by UC San Francisco researchers points to a possible environmental clue in drinking water. Children living in areas with higher levels of naturally occurring lithium were more likely to be diagnosed with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, or WPW, a rare condition involving a particular type of abnormal connection. The findings, published online in The Journal of Clinical Investigation, show an association, but do not establish that lithium causes the condition.

These connections, known as accessory pathways, usually occur in people with no family history of the condition. That suggests environmental exposures during fetal development could play a role. Lithium attracted the researchers’ attention because medicinal doses taken during pregnancy have been associated with an increased risk of congenital heart defects, including Ebstein’s anomaly. This rare defect is frequently accompanied by accessory pathways, prompting the team to investigate whether lithium in drinking water might also be associated with changes in the developing heart.

The researchers analyzed health and water-quality data for more than 2.3 million children in California. Just 686 had a documented WPW diagnosis. Children living in counties with lithium levels in the highest 25% had 71% greater odds of a diagnosis than those in counties with lower levels.

The team then tested its main finding among nearly 2 million children in New York. There, children living in areas with lithium levels above 10 parts per billion also had greater odds of a WPW diagnosis.

Higher lithium levels in California were also associated with palpitations, fainting, and supraventricular tachycardia, or SVT, a rapid heart rhythm that can cause palpitations and other symptoms. Accessory pathways are among the most common causes of SVT. WPW is also associated with a small increased risk of sudden death. Doctors can treat accessory pathways with catheter ablation, a minimally invasive procedure that eliminates the small area of heart tissue responsible for the abnormal electrical connection.

“We’ve known about these pathways for decades, and we know how to treat them, but we haven’t known why people develop them,” said Gregory Marcus, MD, MAS, an endowed professor in atrial fibrillation research in the UCSF Division of Cardiology and senior author of the study. “This is an exciting step because it points to a potential environmental factor that may be modifiable. But we need more research to determine whether lithium is actually contributing to their development.”

The study estimated exposure from the county of residence. Researchers did not know how much lithium individual children or their mothers consumed, and other environmental or genetic factors could help explain the association. Studies in other populations and research that measures exposure during pregnancy more precisely are needed to determine whether lithium plays a causal role.

Marcus said the findings should not alarm people about the safety of their drinking water, including those who are pregnant. Despite the association, WPW was rare in the children studied.

Lithium occurs naturally in groundwater, and its concentration varies widely by location. Groundwater used for drinking water across the United States and elsewhere contains lithium, raising questions about the findings’ potential public health significance beyond California and New York. The researchers said the results underscore the value of collecting environmental data to understand how ordinary exposures may affect health.

“We’re exposed to things in our environment every day, including substances that occur naturally,” Marcus said. “The more precisely we can measure those exposures and connect them with health outcomes, the better we can understand what may be influencing health.”

Lithium in drinking water is not currently regulated in the United States, although the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency requires monitoring through its program for unregulated contaminants. The U.S. Geological Survey also measures lithium in groundwater.

“The next step is to determine whether lithium itself is contributing to the development of these pathways and, if so, how much exposure matters and when during development it matters most,” Marcus said. “That will require studies that can measure exposure much more precisely.”

Reference: “Elevated lithium levels in drinking water are associated with higher prevalence of Wolff-Parkinson-White diagnoses” by Justin T. Teraoka, Anushree Agarwal, Janet J. Tang, Thomas A. Dewland and Gregory M. Marcus, 13 October 2026, The Journal of Clinical Investigation. DOI: 10.1172/JCI205020

#6480. Seabirds get jet lag, too — and it can throw them a bit off course

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Fast east-west flights unlink birds’ internal clocks from the sun, scrambling navigation

A Manx shearwater soars in midflight. New research suggests that a phenomenon akin to jet lag can disrupt the seabirds’ ability to navigate using the sun.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Jet lag isn’t just for travelers hurtling across time zones. Migratory birds may get it, too.

Manx shearwaters (Puffinus puffinus) fly fast enough to experience jet lag, researchers report October 29 in Science. Decades of tracking data from foraging flights revealed that rapid east-west journeys can throw the seabirds’ internal clocks out of sync with local time, causing them to misjudge the sun’s position and veer slightly off course.

For animals crossing vast oceans, the sun can help them determine which direction to fly. But because the sun’s position in the sky changes throughout the day, these animals need an internal clock synchronized with natural local sun time to use it as a compass. This circadian rhythm helps them compensate for the sun’s apparent movement and stay on course.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

But when birds zip east or west, local time shifts faster than their internal clocks might adjust. Scientists have long predicted that this mismatch could confound the birds’ sun-based compasses, but testing the idea in the wild “has seemed impossible until now,” says Tim Guilford, a biologist at the University of Oxford.

Over 20 years, Guilford and colleagues equipped 1,045 breeding Manx shearwaters with miniature GPS trackers. The trackers logged thousands of trips from United Kingdom breeding colonies to feeding grounds up to 1,000 kilometers away. The team focused on the return journeys, isolating 1,837 continuous homeward flights.

Assuming the seabirds’ internal clocks were synchronized with local time at sunrise, the researchers calculated how flights should throw off their sun compass and compared those predictions with GPS tracking data. The birds veered as expected, by as much as 15 degrees from their intended direction.

“But what really surprised us is that the small orientation errors … continue to be visible even when the birds were in sight of presumably familiar land,” Guilford says. While following a coastline, the birds should be able to use it as a guide to keep their course. But they either veered closer to shore or farther out to sea in line with their predicted sun compass errors. The pattern suggests that the birds use the sun compass alongside coastal cues, even when the two point in different directions.

The errors are small enough that they add only a few kilometers to the journey, not enough to prevent the Manx shearwaters from finding their way home.

This navigational tug-of-war excites Sangeeta Rani, a chronobiologist at the University of Lucknow in India. The findings, Rani says, hint at an ability that could serve these feathered fliers well as climate change and human activities alter familiar landscapes: The birds seem to process and integrate multiple navigational cues without relying blindly on any one of them.

“After all, if I have marked a path for myself in the woods, my innate ability is not to mindlessly follow the markings,” Rani says. “It is to find out what’s missing and still find my way back.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

P. Lewin et al. Rapid longitudinal flights cause time shifts and sun compass error. Science. 2026. doi: 10.1126/science.adz2542

#6479. Where to Find the Fastest Delivery for the iPhone Duo

Apple picking is an annual autumn rite, but when it comes to shopping Apple’s first folding phone, retailers have mostly bare branches.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Apple sure underestimated how many people would scramble for an iPhone Duo. Tsunamis of anticipation over the first folding iPhone had built up over years, long before Apple made it official and announced it on October 16, 2026, but how many people would rush to buy a smartphone that starts at $1,999?

It took hardly a day to find out. Perhaps it had something to do with us declaring it the best folding phone yet. During the week prior to the iPhone Duo’s October 23 launch day, when those with a taste for Apple’s latest phone could preorder it on Apple.com, the ship date list stretched into January as people gobbled up the early batch of available units. And on launch day itself, local news everywhere ran story after story about long lines outside Apple stores, with many going home empty-handed before closing time as the Duo quickly sold out.

You can walk into an Apple store and try your luck, although I wouldn’t count on walking out with one in hand. Many Apple stores I’ve checked in big cities have none available for pickup. You can still order one online at Apple, as long as you’re fine with waiting until January 25 to get yours.

You can find the iPhone Duo at Best Buy for Verizon and AT&T. Switching up the color between Night Sky (black) and Star White, or the storage capacity (256GB, 512GB, 1TB, and 2TB), or the carrier, does not change the December 22 shipping or pickup date.

Heading to your local cellular carrier’s retail store may be your best bet for landing an iPhone Duo before Christmas, but like with the Apple Store, I wouldn’t count on it. Verizon casts a wide net for its estimated ship date: December 12–30. Those ordered from T-Mobile won’t make the Christmas cut. As of today, the backordered phone shows a ship date of December 31-January 6. And AT&T may have the longest ship time of all, as its ordering pages offer shipping “As soon as January 6,” which hints that the 6th is the earliest you may expect your AT&T-linked iPhone Duo, but that it may come later.

Interestingly, no matter how I configured each one in any color and storage combination, the estimated ship dates at all three carriers stayed the same. In past years at Apple launches, devices with higher capacities (and correspondingly higher price tags) tended to be available sooner. Not so this time with the iPhone Duo. Just remember that if you buy a phone from one network, it’s not guaranteed to work on another. If you want an unlocked iPhone Duo that’ll work on any cellular network, you’ll have to order it from Apple and practice patience until it ships in early 2027.

Walmart has listed product pages for the iPhone Duo since Apple announced it, but I’ve yet to see anybody actually able to order one there. I’ve kept a near-daily eye on the Walmart page, though, and every combination of color, carrier, and storage option has been out of stock and unavailable to backorder since the iPhone Duo’s debut.

If you’re on the fence, don’t expect the waitlist to shorten while you wring your hands. Occasionally, ship dates for hot, newly released devices move up as retailers receive new batches, but I’ve been keeping a close eye on the iPhone Duo for the past three weeks and haven’t seen that happen at any retailer, including Apple itself. The ship dates we’ve provided here are current as of today. They can only get longer from here.

#6478. Why do the faintest galaxies around the Milky Way all hold about the same amount of iron?

Simulations suggest the faintest galaxies near the Milky Way share one iron level because a single giant first star exploded in each.

Smaller galaxies usually hold less iron, so the faintest ones circling the Milky Way should be the poorest of all. They aren’t. Below a certain size, they all carry about the same small share of iron, and computer models have struggled for years to explain why.

New simulations suggest an answer. In most of these tiny galaxies, the iron came from a single explosion of one giant star from the Universe’s first generation.

The simulations come from MEGATRON, a project led by Martin Rey of the University of Bath with collaborators at the University of Chicago and the Institut d’Astrophysique de Paris (IAP).

They’re computer models rather than telescope observations, and the result depends on assumptions that remain uncertain about the first stars.

Every carbon, oxygen and iron atom around us was made inside a star, Rey said. The very first stars formed from hydrogen and helium alone, and their explosions started that process.

In an interview with Earth.com, Rey explained why the oldest surviving stars matter. “Those old stars are basically a fossil record, preserving the chemical fingerprints of events that happened over 13 billion years ago,” he said.

Many of those stars belong to ultra-faint dwarf galaxies, the dimmest galaxies orbiting the Milky Way. Each holds no more than about 100,000 times the Sun’s mass in stars. They stopped making new stars long ago, so astronomers treat them as relics of the early universe.

Among larger dwarf galaxies, iron drops as size drops. For the smallest ones, however, that trend flattens out. Their stars average roughly one three-hundredth of the Sun’s share of iron, and astronomers call this the iron plateau.

Earlier simulations had trouble giving such small galaxies that much iron.

The MEGATRON team simulated a patch of the early Universe that will grow into a galaxy with the Milky Way’s mass. The program follows gas, starlight and chemistry at once, keeping count of more than 80 kinds of atoms and molecules.

That matters because the project aims to connect two views of the early Universe. The James Webb Space Telescope sees young galaxies directly, while old stars nearby keep a chemical record of the same era.

Four versions started from the same point. Each used different assumptions about the second generation of stars, which formed after the first stars had added heavier elements to the gas. All four used the same recipe for the first stars.

Together, the runs produced more than 500 small galaxies. They end about 12 billion years before the present.

In all four versions, most of the smallest galaxies ended up with the iron level astronomers measure in real ones. About 78 percent fell inside the plateau’s range, between a thousandth and a hundredth of the Sun’s share.

Since only the second-generation recipe changed between runs, the authors took that as a sign that the first stars set the pattern.

Most of the small galaxies had exactly one first-generation star explode inside them. Those on the plateau mostly got their iron from stars, between 160 and 300 times the Sun’s mass, which blow themselves apart.

Each of those explosions makes about five times the Sun’s mass in iron, according to the published estimates the team used.

Asked what surprised him most, Rey told Earth.com, “In our simulations, this plateau falls out naturally from the physics of the first stars.” The team hadn’t gone looking for it.

“The simulations were never designed to reproduce it and we had not even planned to explore or look into this question,” he said. One of his collaborators suggested making the figure out of curiosity.

An explosion that powerful can blast its debris out of a small galaxy. In MEGATRON, that mostly didn’t happen.

Ultraviolet light from the young central galaxy kept gas from forming the hydrogen molecules it needs to cool down and collapse into stars. So the first stars couldn’t form in the smallest clumps of matter.

They formed instead in heavier clumps of dark matter and gas, about 10 million times the Sun’s mass, with enough gravity to hold on to the debris. Later stars then formed from that iron-enriched gas.

The authors checked this with a simple calculation. Spreading five Suns’ worth of iron through the gas in one of those clumps matches the plateau’s average level.

A lighter giant star, around 140 times the Sun’s mass, makes about a tenth as much iron, which leaves its galaxy well below the plateau.

About 22 percent of the small simulated galaxies fall below the plateau, with less than a thousandth of the Sun’s share of iron. No ultra-faint galaxy measured so far is that poor.

If a fifth of them really were, the chance of finding none among the 38 measured would be about 0.02 percent, the authors calculated. That counts against the prediction.

Still, the census is thin. Many of these galaxies have iron measured in only a few stars. One of them, Pictor II, averages right at the plateau’s lower edge, and it holds a star with almost no iron.

Both groups would still exist today, according to the team’s forecast. Most small galaxies get torn apart and spread into the faint cloud of stars around a galaxy like the Milky Way, called the halo.

In a companion study led by Anatole Storck, the team found that 75 to 80 percent of the first stars’ remains end up there, Rey said.

“So the debris of the very first generation of stars is, quite literally, still out there around us,” Rey said.

MEGATRON’s plateau rests on three assumptions, and the authors wrote that each is uncertain. Ultraviolet light from the young galaxy has to be strong. The first stars have to be mostly giants. And each giant explosion has to make a lot of iron.

That second assumption is debated, since some newer models suggest the first stars were lighter. The simulations also make much less nitrogen than astronomers measure in real old stars, and the simulated young galaxy may not match the Milky Way’s early history.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory is expected to find many new faint galaxies, and the next generation of very large telescopes should measure the iron in their stars.

Rey has been awarded 40 million hours of processing time on the U.K.’s national supercomputers for the next round. He compared that to running five million laptops for a year.

With them, his team will test “which assumptions about the first stars match local data, and more importantly which do not,” he said.

One galaxy found below the plateau would fit the prediction. If surveys keep finding none, the first stars may have been even heavier than assumed, or the plateau has another cause.

The full study was published in the journal The Open Journal of Astrophysics.

Researchers have created a self-charging toothbrush that helps fight the bacteria linked to cavities and gum disease while preventing plaque buildup.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A toothbrush that generates its own electricity with every stroke could offer a new way to fight the microbes behind cavities and gum disease.

Conventional toothbrushes rely on physical scrubbing to remove plaque from teeth and gums. But even after a thorough brush, some bacteria remain and begin rebuilding plaque. To solve that problem, researchers have developed a self-powered toothbrush that converts the friction of brushing into an electrical charge. That electricity is intended to zap the plaque-promoting bacteria and keep them from colonizing teeth.

"It's great to have new approaches that actually enhance the effect of mechanical cleaning," said Nicholas Jakubovics, an oral microbiologist at Newcastle University in the U.K. who was not involved in the study. "The idea that the toothbrush surface itself is actively doing something is really interesting."

The experimental brush has bristles made from polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), a plastic that generates electricity when bent; these types of energy-producing materials are called piezoelectric. As the bristles flex during brushing, they produce an electrical charge that then triggers chemical reactions in saliva and water. These reactions release reactive oxygen species (ROS), which are highly reactive molecules that can damage bacterial cells.

Even when the bristles are not being used to brush, they carry a faint surface charge that helps prevent bacteria from clinging to the brush head when the toothbrush isn't in use, the team reported Wednesday (Nov. 4) in the journal Science Advances.

In laboratory tests where the toothbrush was used on isolated germs, its electrified bristles killed more than half of the Streptococcus mutans bacteria present. These microbes contribute to tooth decay. By comparison, nylon bristles killed just 9% of the bacteria. They also reduced levels of Porphyromonas gingivalis, a bacterium linked to gum disease, by up to 78%, while nylon brushes reduced them by less than 8%.

When the researchers added an antioxidant — a compound that neutralizes ROS — the new toothbrush's antibacterial effect largely disappeared, highlighting that the ROS are likely the key to its effects.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team also found that the activity of certain genes in both S. mutans and P. gingivalis fell after exposure to the electrified bristles. These genes are involved in making ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters — molecular pumps that help shuttle essential nutrients across bacterial cell membranes. The researchers suspect that disrupting this machinery makes it harder for these microbes to survive and cling to teeth.

The new toothbrush still needs to be tested in further safety trials.

But Jakubovics was not convinced by that part of the team's explanation. "ABC transporters transport all sorts of different things," he said, adding that the findings did not clearly show how changes in these genes affected the bacteria.

The researchers also tested the new brush against plaque biofilms — hardy communities of bacteria that stick together and cling to tooth surfaces. For the experiment, they grew human dental plaque on cow tooth enamel and found that the brush removed more than 99% of the biofilm, outperforming a regular nylon brush.

Finally, the team moved to humans, putting the brush to the test in 115 adults with gum inflammation or tooth decay. These study participants were randomly assigned to use either the new toothbrushes or traditional nylon-bristled brushes twice a day for three months. (The study didn't note whether participants noticed a difference in sensation when using the electrified brushes.)

By the end of the trial, the participants who used the electrified bristles had less plaque, less gum inflammation and less bleeding than the participants who used ordinary brushes. Plaque samples also showed that the people who used electrified brushes had lower levels of bacteria associated with oral disease and higher levels of beneficial bacteria, which have previously been reported to suppress harmful oral bacteria and support oral health.

The researchers think that the disease-linked bacteria may have relatively fragile cell membranes, making them more vulnerable to damage from ROS than the beneficial bacteria. That's a theory that requires further study, though, so it's not completely clear how selective the brush is against plaque-causing bacteria.

In a test of the toothbrush's durability, the PVDF bristles retained their structure and electrical properties over three months of simulated use. Lab-grown mouse cells repeatedly exposed to brush material showed no signs of damage, and brushing on cow tooth enamel did not increase surface roughness. However, these tests cannot establish whether repeated use of these brushes is safe for humans.

"We would want to make sure that it is safe on the tissues for long-term use," Jakubovics said. He noted that, in lab tests, bacteria are grown directly on the bristles and exposed to their electricity for hours, "whereas in reality, in the mouth, your bristle is only in contact with the tooth or oral tissue for a very short time."

The trial with humans provides some insight into how the brush works in real life, but it was relatively small. Larger studies will be needed to find out whether the toothbrush offers a meaningful advantage over conventional brushes. For now, Jakubovics sees the recent study as just a proof of concept; more information and more convincing clinical data are still needed, he emphasized.

#6476. Lightweight packaging has a surprising recycling problem

Lightweight packaging may be more likely to end up in the trash because its flimsy feel affects how people judge its remaining value.

People often say they recycle, but their actual choices can depend on how an empty package feels.

A new study suggests that lightweight, crinkly bottles are more likely to land in the trash than sturdier ones.

Lyndsay Loomer and Sarah Whitley from the University of Georgia investigated this pattern across five studies.

The researchers found that packaging density is a powerful and largely unexamined driver of recycling behavior.

Lightweight packaging, the kind increasingly common as companies trim material costs under sustainability mandates, is significantly more likely to end up in a landfill than its heavier counterpart.

In some cases, it was 92 percent more likely to be trashed.

Lead author Lyndsay Loomer came to this question from the inside. Before earning her doctorate at Georgia’s Terry College of Business, she worked in brand marketing for a beverage company in Texas.

She watched her firm introduce lightweight, thin-walled bottles to reduce plastic use in the late 2010s.

Consumers bought them without complaint. But she kept thinking about what happened afterward.

“As I became more familiar with sustainability literature, I thought if the package feels low quality and like trash – what if they’re more likely to throw it away?” Loomer said.

“Then we’re kind of shooting ourselves in the foot, right?”

“It’s related to this idea of waste aversion. We don’t want to get rid of things that we feel have more useful life or value. And we infer a lot of that through the material properties – the weight or feel – of whatever item it is.”

The team tested this intuition across five studies combining field observation and controlled experiments.

The pilot study capitalized on a real-world packaging change: Coca-Cola’s Dasani brand transitioning to a lighter bottle in spring 2022, reducing plastic density by over 40 percent.

Researchers distributed both bottle types at a campus speaker event and audited the disposal bins afterward. The low-density bottles landed in the trash at a measurably higher rate.

Zero high-density bottles were trashed; 4.76 percent of the lightweight ones were.

The pilot was small, so the team went further. They audited every trash and recycling bin on the first floor of Georgia’s business school complex over a full week.

They cataloged 172 recyclable plastic containers and weighed each one.

Containers found in recycling bins had an average density 60 percent higher than those found in the trash.

Each additional gram per fluid ounce of density increased a container’s odds of being recycled by nearly tenfold.

“When you look at disposal behavior, it’s not enough to just have people indicate how they will dispose of an item,” Whitley said.

“You have to see if they’re actually going to do it. Everyone says they’re going to recycle because there’s a lot of social desirability bias there. We had to have evidence of people doing it.”

That evidence held across materials. Subsequent experiments replicated the density effect with paper.

In each case, the pattern was the same: lighter means more disposable, in both senses of the word.

The mechanism the researchers identified runs through two distinct judgments people make almost instantaneously at the moment of disposal.

The first is a value assessment: flimsy packaging reads as lower quality and therefore lower value.

The second is emotional – what researchers call waste aversion, the discomfort of throwing something away that still seems useful.

Heavier packaging triggers more of that discomfort than lightweight packaging.

Participants in the controlled experiments weren’t told to consider weight, suggesting that packaging density can influence disposal without explicit prompts.

The more practically useful finding may be what happened when the researchers tried to interrupt this process.

In Study 4, they added a simple printed message to a low-density paper envelope: “You may be done with this envelope, but it still has value.”

That single line increased the likelihood of recycling the envelope by 52 percent.

“Material lightweighting seems like a good idea on the surface because people don’t really care about it so much from a buying perspective, it lowers costs, and it’s sustainable,” Whitley said.

“But manufacturers need to think one step further.”

The implication for companies is pointed. Lightweighting reduces material use and transportation emissions on the production side.

Lower recycling rates could offset some of those benefits. The findings highlight why companies need to consider disposal behavior alongside material use and transportation.

The researchers describe this as a form of unintentional greenwashing: sustainable at the factory, unsustainable at the bin.

“If we’re not examining the downstream consumer implications of manufacturing changes, we’re not going to move forward in terms of some of these sustainability goals,” Loomer said.

The findings suggest that recycling behavior depends on more than people’s intentions. The physical properties of packaging can also influence which bin they choose.

Recycling rates in the U.S. have stagnated for years despite widespread awareness campaigns and strong public support for recycling.

The solution may not require heavier packaging.

A brief message about an item’s remaining value could help companies reduce material use while encouraging consumers to recycle.

The study is published in the Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science.
