#6458. Dirty air actually breaks down the smell of flowers and stops bees and moths from finding their food

Ozone and nitrogen oxides cut pollinators' ability to find flowers by about half, and ozone will stay high until around 2050 as fuels change.

A bee finds a flower the way you find a bakery, by following the smell. Exhaust from cars and machines breaks those scent molecules apart in the air.

A review of 22 experiments now puts a number on the damage. Polluted air cut how well pollinators found and used flowers by roughly half, and two pollutants together cut it by more than two thirds.

The surprise is in the timing. Even as the world burns less fossil fuel, one of those two pollutants, ozone, isn’t expected to drop below today’s levels until after about 2050.

James Ryalls at the University of Reading led the review with colleagues Jacob Bishop and Carol Wagstaff. In an interview with Earth.com, Ryalls said the result that surprised him most was what the two gases did together.

“It was the first time this interaction had been quantified for pollinators,” he said.

Flowers advertise with chemicals that drift off their petals, and pollinators follow those chemicals to the food. Ozone and nitrogen oxides react with the scent molecules in the air. They break some down and change others, so the trail an insect is following gets weaker and stranger.

Researchers have also linked the gases to duller antennae, poorer learning and memory, and weaker colonies in bees. However, the review ranks that direct damage behind the scent damage.

Ozone is a gas that forms in sunlit air from other pollutants. Nitrogen oxides come mostly from engines, and diesel engines above all.

Ryalls’s team pulled together every experiment it could find that measured flower pollinators in clean air against polluted air. There were 22 studies in all, with 87 comparisons between them.

Most used honeybees or bumblebees. A few used a hawkmoth, a fig wasp or a mix of wild insects, and the setups ranged from lab chambers to greenhouses to open fields with pollutants piped in.

Across those studies, increased ozone lowered pollinator performance by an average of 42 percent, and increased nitrogen oxides lowered it by 46 percent.

Performance here covers three things: how well insect pollinators found flowers, how well they fed on them, and how many turned up.

Only three research teams tested both gases at once, and in those experiments the average loss was 68 percent. That is worse than either gas alone, but well short of the 88 percent you would get by simply adding the two. The gases don’t stack.

Ryalls had an explanation for the gap. “This reflects real atmospheric chemistry, where ozone and nitrogen oxides can partially react with and offset each other,” he told Earth.com.

In the three studies that measured each gas and the pair against the same clean-air control, the extra harm from adding the second gas was smaller still.

The damage was not spread evenly across what insects do. Searching efficiency, the measure of how well a pollinator locates flowers, fell by 67 percent on average. Feeding, once an insect reached a flower, and the number of insects present changed little.

Ryalls said he wanted people to notice that pattern. The insects were not sickened so much as lost.

Specialists have it worst. A bee that visits many kinds of flower can switch cues when one scent breaks down. An insect tied to one plant, like the tobacco hawkmoth or the yucca moth, has no backup.

Timing matters too. Ozone peaks in daylight, when bees and butterflies are out. That is bad timing for crops such as almonds and oilseed rape, whose flowers open in daylight when ozone peaks.

In contrast, nitrogen oxides are often highest at night, when moths do their pollinating. So the two groups face different pollutants, and cutting one gas doesn’t protect both.

Burning less fossil fuel cuts nitrogen oxides. Ozone, however, is made in the air from several ingredients, including methane and carbon monoxide, and those stay high for longer.

Under the middle-of-the-road emissions path used by the IPCC, the authors expect ground-level ozone to stay elevated through mid-century and only drop below today’s levels after about 2050.

On a high-emissions path, ozone is predicted to keep rising into the 2060s. It will only fall below today’s levels near the end of the century.

Diesel vehicles complicate the picture further, because a diesel sold today can stay on the road for more than 20 years. Britain’s decision to push its ban on new gasoline and diesel cars from 2030 to 2035 is the kind of delay the authors said will stretch the hard years out.

One oddity cuts the other way: in cities, nitrogen oxides break down some of the ozone, a buffer that fades in the countryside where there is less exhaust.

“Most of the food we grow depends on healthy pollinators, so protecting them from pollution cannot wait until 2050,” Ryalls said.

Asked by Earth.com what gardeners and farmers can do, Ryalls said cutting local nitrogen oxide emissions would help most.

He suggested replacing older diesel machinery and generators, keeping high-emission equipment idle during peak flowering, expanding green spaces, and letting lawns run wild and flower.

The evidence is lopsided. Of the 22 studies, 19 were done in Europe and 16 used bees or their relatives. That matters because about 70 percent of crop species get some benefit from insect pollination. The countries with the dirtiest air, such as India and China, are the ones likely to be hit hardest.

Flies, beetles and most moths are barely tested, and the tropics, where pollution is often heavier and more insects are generalists, are almost absent from research studies.

The doses were high as well: the average ozone level in the experiments was 161 parts per billion, more than twice the U.S. limit of 70. Harm clearly happened at those levels, but the studies can’t say where it begins.

Whether it starts at a sharp threshold or builds gradually is still an open question, and so is where a safe level might be.

Ryalls wants the next experiments run where the air is already dirty. “I’d like to test these effects in higher-pollution regions and tropical systems, where baseline pollutant levels are often higher and pollinator communities differ,” he said.

His group is also testing treatments that could boost the scents flowers give off, to help insects find them in polluted air.

The full study was published in the journal Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment.

It's the end of an era: NASA's Swift telescope has reached the conclusion of its nearly 22-year mission, burning up in Earth's atmosphere after studying some of the universe's most powerful and mysterious events.

According to NASA, the spacecraft reentered the atmosphere at "7:39 a.m. EST Wednesday over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia, at approximately 3.4 degrees north latitude and 98.6 degrees east longitude." NASA expected most of the telescope's structure to burn up during its passage through Earth's atmosphere, estimating a 1-in-2,100 chance of any surviving debris falling over a populated area. No damage or injuries have been reported.

Weighing approximately 3,200 pounds (1,450 kilograms), the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory was initially designed for a two-year mission, but it far exceeded expectations. Over two decades, Swift became an important tool in the study of gamma-ray bursts, supernovas, black holes and other cosmic phenomena.

Launched in November 2004, Swift was designed to detect gamma-ray bursts, powerful explosions that occur throughout the universe. Its three onboard telescopes let scientists observe cosmic events across different wavelengths, including ultraviolet, optical and X-ray light. The telescope could swivel to focus on different sky targets in a matter of minutes, allowing it to rapidly follow up on sudden events like supernova explosions.

NASA estimates that Swift's scientific observations have contributed to approximately 7,000 research papers, leaving behind an extensive collection that scientists can continue studying for years.

Swift's return was driven by atmospheric drag, which eventually slowed the spacecraft and caused its orbit to decay. Increased solar activity intensified the drag, thus accelerating the space telescope's descent toward Earth.

Earlier this year, NASA explored an ambitious rescue mission to extend Swift's operational life. In August 2026, a privately developed robotic spacecraft built by Katalyst Space Technologies was intended to rendezvous with Swift and boost it into a higher orbit. However, the mission failed after launching, leaving the observatory on its path toward reentry.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

NASA officially ended Swift's scientific operations on Oct. 20 after its declining altitude made observations too difficult. For NASA and the broader astronomy community, Swift's story is a reminder that even missions designed to last just a few years can fundamentally change our understanding of our universe.

#6456. Young children are fascinated by sharks – so why are older kids more fearful?

A survey finds most children like sharks, but older kids express more fear, raising questions about how views of these animals develop.

Sharks have a scary reputation, but many young children like them. Some think they look cool, while others like the way they swim.

A survey of parents of 374 children aged two to 12 found that 69% of the children liked sharks. Older children were more likely to say sharks scared them.

Brianna Le Busque, an environmental psychologist at Adelaide University‘s School of Physics, Chemistry and Earth Sciences, led the study. Parents asked the questions and recorded their children’s answers.

“What’s really interesting is that most of the children in our study actually liked sharks, and many were fascinated by them,” Le Busque said.

People are often less willing to protect animals they fear or dislike. That makes children’s early views of sharks worth understanding.

The few earlier studies on this topic mostly found fear. In a 2020 study, five-year-olds chose a face to show how a shark photo made them feel, and most chose a fearful face.

But those studies left out toddlers. They also usually asked children about sharks alongside other animals, which may have made sharks seem less appealing next to dogs, horses and dolphins.

For the new study, 323 parents took an online survey in 2024. They asked their children what sharks do, what they look like and whether they liked them.

Parents wrote down the answers word for word and noted any hand gestures. They asked brothers and sisters separately so they couldn’t copy each other.

The team counted a child as expressing fear if they called sharks scary, said they were afraid or clearly showed fear another way.

Saying sharks bite or are dangerous didn’t count, because knowing an animal can hurt you doesn’t always mean you fear it.

The most common reason children gave for liking sharks was that they were cool. One four-year-old girl said, “sharks are very cool.”

When describing sharks, 44% mentioned teeth and 33% said they were big. Most talked about sharks swimming and eating, although about one in five said they hurt people.

Some children mixed facts with imagination. A six-year-old boy asked whether sharks were reptiles, then answered himself, “no they’re not, they’re dinosaurs.”

Children who disliked sharks most often said sharks hurt people. One 10-year-old boy explained, “because they could eat me.”

Overall, 13.9% of the children described sharks as scary or expressed fear of them.

Older children did this more often, and the team’s analysis suggested the pattern was unlikely to be due to chance.

“But as children got older, we saw an increase in associations between sharks and fear,” Le Busque said.

“That raises important questions about what children are learning about sharks as they grow up and the role that society, media and other influences might play.”

The team found no clear difference between boys and girls or between children in Australia, the U.S. and the U.K., where most participants lived. How often children went into the ocean made no clear difference either.

The survey compared different age groups. It did not follow the same children as they grew up, so it couldn’t show how any one child’s feelings changed.

Books were the most common way children had come across sharks. About 65% had read shark books or had someone read them aloud.

Another 59% had seen sharks at an aquarium, and 38% had watched TV shows featuring them. About a quarter had seen shark films, including Finding Nemo and Jaws.

Some 13% had sung “Baby Shark,” which became YouTube’s most-viewed video in 2020.

The researchers think these experiences may help explain why many children liked sharks.

Watching sharks swim among other fish at an aquarium, for example, may help children see sharks as more than dangerous animals.

Films may leave a different impression. Older children were more likely to mention Jaws, a film long linked to negative views of sharks and even government responses to shark bites.

Finding Nemo also mixes friendly and frightening images. Bruce appears as a friendly shark trying to stop eating fish, but becomes aggressive when he smells a single drop of blood.

“Sharks are often portrayed in very dramatic and sensational ways, particularly when there is a shark bite or in popular films,” Le Busque said.

Still, the study did not test whether films changed children’s feelings about sharks. The researchers say that needs more study.

Among parents, 44% reported low fear of sharks and 30% reported high fear. Many less fearful parents said they lived far from sharks or could avoid them.

One parent wrote, “The same reason I’m not afraid of earthquakes – I don’t live in an area where they reside.”

The team found no clear link between parents’ fear and their children’s fear.

Some parents said sharks weren’t an everyday threat, which may give children few chances to see their parents react fearfully.

A larger study might find a small link, the researchers noted.

Parents may have influenced their children’s answers or misunderstood them. The researchers accepted that risk because toddlers can’t complete a survey alone.

Views of sharks also differ across cultures, and shark populations vary around the world. Only 14 children in the study were 12, and none were teenagers.

Children’s fear might ease during their teens as they learn more. But strong fears that start in childhood can also last into adulthood.

A recent review found that people who know more about sharks tend to fear them less. Earlier research also linked direct experiences with sharks to greater tolerance of them.

In another study, people who swam with sharks were more likely to report helping sharks two years later.

These findings suggest that learning and positive experiences may help, though they don’t tell us how each child’s feelings will change.

The researchers suggest using lessons and media to show children the many kinds of sharks, helping balance stories built around fear.

“Children are clearly capable of seeing sharks as fascinating, interesting animals, rather than simply something to be afraid of,” Le Busque said.

“Education and positive experiences could be really important in helping children understand sharks as diverse marine animals and appreciate the important role they play in our oceans.”

To learn whether fear fades or lasts, researchers will need to follow the same children into their teens.

They also want future studies to use a standard set of questions about fear, making the results easier to compare.

The study is published in the journal Human Dimensions of Wildlife.

#6455. A 400-Year-Old Mass Murderer Led a Brutal Mutiny—and Became the First Corporate Psychopath

A modern psychopathy test, applied to a 1629 shipwreck, uncovers the dark origins of toxic bosses.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

When you try to envision a “corporate psychopath,” the kind of individual who blends charm towards their superiors and sadism towards their subordinates to rise through the corporate ranks, who comes to mind?

Actually, don’t say a specific name. These guys can be very litigious, so let’s just focus on the vague and the deceased. You’re probably picturing a man in an expensive business suit, maybe having a loud, hyperbolic conversation on an oversized 1980s cell phone. Maybe he’s monologuing about how “greed is good,” or how they’re “gonna need to send the National Guard to take him out, ‘cause he’s not goin’ nowhere.” Perhaps the corporate psychopath you have in mind is busy fretting about whether his business card has lettering in Romalian or Silian Rail.

In other words, short of someone you’ve seen on the news, or in your own boardroom, your mental image of a corporate psychopath probably comes from the movies.

You may want to revise that. That’s because a new study suggests that the original corporate psycho predates the 1980s stock market antiheroes of the movies you love. He actually predates movies entirely. In fact, he died before the city of Boston was ever founded.

In a study published in the Asian Journal of Business Ethics, Clive Roland Boddy, an author and pioneer in the study of corporate psychopathy, has identified Jeronimous Cornelisz of the Dutch East India Company as perhaps the earliest documented example of a corporate psychopath. To understand why, one must delve into the dark story of the 1629 Batavia shipwreck and its mutinous aftermath.

The Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie, translated as Dutch East India Company and abbreviated as VOC, was a fairly unique venture in the business world at the dawn of the 17th century. At the time, expeditions for goods and resources were often funded individually, and the companies behind them lasted only as long as a single voyage. The VOC changed that by merging 12 existing “pre-companies” within the Dutch Republic into a permanent company that would not only fund spice expeditions but also manage supply and stabilize the market. Shares of the VOC could be publicly purchased and traded by Dutch citizens at various aftermarkets throughout the Republic, including the predecessor to the Euronext Amsterdam, arguably making the VOC the world’s first multinational corporation.

In some ways, the VOC resembled the multinational corporations we know today, with the same ruthless efficiency. Yet the world around it lacked the kind of laws and regulations that are at least supposed to keep the corporations of our modern world in check. In fact, the Dutch government backed the VOC entirely, allowing the company to have a monopoly over the Asian spice trade. It was an environment that favored the bold, the ambitious, and the unscrupulous. It was an environment that allowed a man like Jeronimus Cornelisz to seize his moment.

“Psychopaths have a narcissistic and grossly inflated view of their self-worth and importance,” Mike Dash writes in his book Batavia’s Graveyard: The True Story of the Mad Heretic Who Led History’s Bloodiest Mutiny, “...a truly astonishing egocentricity and sense of entitlement, and see themselves as the centre of the universe, as superior beings who are justified in living according to their own rules.” It’s unclear exactly when Jeronimus Cornelisz created his own set of rules to live by, whether in his poorly-documented childhood, or when he took up his apothecary trade some time in the 1620s and began battling with his local town council.

What we know is that by 1628, the death of his child and the subsequent scandal it invited (the three-month old had died of syphilis, and Cornelisz tried to argue the child had contracted it from a wet nurse rather than his own wife) led to the Dutchman selling his business and taking a job with the VOC. In October 1628, the Batavia left port in the Netherlands on a trip to the Dutch East Indies, with commodore Francisco Pelsaert as its commander, Ariaen Jacobsz as its skipper, and Cornelisz as a junior officer.

Pelsaert’s journal recounts that on June 4, 1629, “I was lying in my bunk feeling ill and felt suddenly, with a rough terrible movement, the bumping of the ship’s rudder, and immediately after that I felt the ship held up in her course against the rocks, so that I fell out of my bunk.” The vessel had run aground on Western Australia’s Morning Reef while Jacobsz was at the helm, and roughly 100 of the 340 people aboard the ship were killed in the collision. To date, there’s still fierce debate over whether the Batavia crashed “by design or accident,” as by this time, Cornelisz had charmed his way into Jacobsz’ esteem, and in doing so, had convinced him that a mutiny was necessary to depose Pelsaert.

Either way, as some of the roughly 180 survivors disembarked for the nearby islands, leaving only 70 (including Cornelisz) aboard, an opportunity arose for the original “hostile takeover.”

Cornelisz had originally been among the 70 or so who remained aboard the Batavia, but after nine days, he made his way to nearby Beacon Island. He found the survivors stranded there to be starving, dying of thirst, and feeling abandoned, since Pelsaert had left with the other officers in search of supplies and aid. Seizing his moment, Cornelisz stepped into the leadership vacuum, amassing a group of loyal enforcers, and stripping the now subordinate survivors of any means by which to fend for, or defend, themselves.

Cornelisz began a reign of terror that lasted more than two months, overseeing the execution of those deemed “too weak,” as well as those he thought capable of overpowering him. Supplies were hoarded for his loyalists, while those outside of his circle were dispatched in ever more public and brutal ways. His roughly 40 man cadre killed an estimated 100-125 men, women, and children, and the survivors didn’t fare much better.

“Furthermore, when the most murders had been committed,” Pelseart would write in his journal, “...they shared the women who remained, or rather whom they had meant to stay alive.” Cornelisz, who had singled out Lucretia Jansz for his own ill-intent, “made several articles to which the women had to be put on oath if they wanted to remain alive, that they had to be obedient to the men in all that they should desire of them.”

While all of this may read like the barbaric horrors of a bygone age, befitting a pirate’s pillaging more than a modern boardroom, Boddy’s study found that when Cornelisz’s actions are viewed through the prism of The Psychopathy Measure–Management Research Version (PM–MRV), a ten-item model he previously developed to identify contemporary corporate psychopaths, the mutinous, murderous junior officer of the VOC checked off every box.

Boddy’s article doesn’t recontextualize Cornelisz’s crimes to exonerate the man; there’s little debate that Jeronimus was a psychopath of some stripe. Nor does Boddy suggest that the existence of the VOC created or caused Cornelisz’s monstrous urges. Rather, it emphasizes that the profit motive built into the structure of the VOC “would have been too great, even for a careful primary psychopath” to resist. This analysis demonstrates that corporate psychopaths as we know them today “have been active since the start of the World’s first stock exchange, and first multinational shareholder-owned corporations.” What unites Cornelisz with the less-overtly-murderous corporate psychopaths we encounter today is the manner in which they both “utilise a similar modus operandi across the centuries and are motivated by greed, self-aggrandisement, and the desire to hurt, dominate and control others.”

In other words, to subvert a quote lamented by another lunatic, Billy Loomis in 1996’s Scream: corporations don’t create psychos. Corporations make psychos more creative.

#6454. Intensive breathing exercises can create psychedelic ‘tripping’ effects by changing how the brain talks to itself

Intensive breathwork cut brain blood flow by about 45 percent in MRI scans, yet the depth of the altered state tracked brain networks, not the drop.

People who practice intensive breathwork (fast, nonstop breathing) for an hour describe something close to a psychedelic trip. They recount vivid mental imagery, a sense of unity with the universe, and no drug involved.

Inside an MRI scanner, the brain lost nearly half its usual blood supply during that experience. Yet how far the blood flow fell had nothing to do with how deep the experience went.

Christian Schmitz led the work at the Central Institute of Mental Health in Mannheim, Germany. His colleagues came from the Medical Faculty Mannheim of Heidelberg University and the MIND Foundation in Berlin.

His team scanned the brains of 30 experienced breathwork practitioners during a single session, with no comparison group, so the findings are preliminary.

“Many people who practice intensive breathwork report profound changes in perception and self-experience, yet the underlying brain mechanisms remain poorly understood,” Schmitz said.

“Our study suggests that these experiences are linked not only to marked changes in cerebral blood flow, but also to alterations in how key brain networks communicate.”

Breathing hard and fast for a long time removes carbon dioxide from the blood faster than the body makes it.

Carbon dioxide is one of the main signals that keeps the brain’s small blood vessels open. When it drops, those vessels tighten and less blood gets through.

The team measured blood flow through the brain’s grey matter at the moment each person rated the experience strongest.

At this point, blood flow had fallen from about 30 to about 16 milliliters per 100 grams of tissue per minute. That is a drop of about 45 percent, which is a large change for something a person does on purpose.

Earlier studies have reported signs of the brain not getting enough oxygen when flow falls by 50 to 60 percent. The average here came close to that limit and stayed below it.

A 2025 study of the same kind of intensive breathwork measured a drop of 41.6 percent, and Schmitz’s team wrote that the two results agree.

The 30 volunteers were between 26 and 64 years old, and half were women. Most had practiced intensive breathwork for one to three years, typically less than once a month.

Anyone with a history of a psychiatric or neurological disorder was left out, and so was anyone who had taken a psychedelic in the previous three months.

Each person lay in the scanner and breathed in a continuous circle, with no pause between breaths, for as long as they chose. That ran from about 36 to 96 minutes. Music played the whole time, either their own or the study’s.

Every 12 minutes, the room light came on and the person pressed one of four buttons to rate the experience against the strongest breathwork session of their life.

Medical staff supervised every session, and monitoring continued for at least an hour afterward.

The experiences were strong: on the four-point scale, the average rating at the peak was 3.5, and the most common answer was the top mark.

Within an hour of the session’s end, each person filled in a standard questionnaire on altered states. The profile that came back was dominated by a sense of boundlessness and a drop in alertness, with milder visual changes.

Psychedelics produce a closely similar profile, the authors wrote. The scores were lower, though, than people typically report after a moderate to high dose of LSD or psilocybin.

A person whose blood flow fell the most was no more likely to report an intense experience than a person whose flow fell the least. The size of the drop predicted neither the button ratings during the session nor the questionnaire scores afterward.

One reading, the authors wrote, is that the drop works like a threshold. Once blood flow falls far enough, altered states become possible, and falling further doesn’t deepen them.

The team also looked at the default mode network, a set of brain regions that are active together when a person is resting and thinking about themselves.

Psilocybin and LSD reliably weaken the coordination inside that network, and the team expected intensive breathwork to do the same.

Resting scans before and after the session showed no overall change in how tightly those regions worked together. But the people whose network connections weakened the most reported the most intense altered states.

The team found that link under one way of cleaning the scan data and not under another, so they called it tentative. The drop in blood flow didn’t predict the network change either.

So the authors described two partly separate things: a brain getting far less blood and, in some people, a reorganizing network that goes with the experience itself.

The team presented the work at the ECNP Congress in Munich in October.

Everyone in the study was an experienced practitioner, so how a first-timer’s brain responds is an open question.

The network scans were taken after the breathing stopped, not during it, because the chest and head movement of circular breathing ruins that kind of scan. Any change that faded quickly was missed.

The team didn’t measure carbon dioxide in the breath, and there was no comparison session of plain rest. Music played throughout, which the authors wrote can change the same network on its own.

Hana Adolphi at the Central Institute of Mental Health co-coordinated the study and is a co-author on the publication. “Breathwork is a legal, inexpensive and non-pharmacological intervention that may provide a valuable tool for studying altered states of consciousness,” she said.

“Nevertheless, this was a relatively small study, and the findings should be considered preliminary. Larger studies will be needed to determine whether these brain changes have clinical relevance,” she added.

Whether the network change happens during the breathing itself, rather than after it, is the question this design couldn’t answer.

The authors wrote that future studies need scanning methods that can cope with the motion of hard breathing, and a plain resting session to compare against.

The full study was published in the journal Progress in Neuro-Psychopharmacology and Biological Psychiatry.

#6453. This Halloween, amateur astronomers may be in for a dwarf planet treat

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Astronomers also have their eyes on objects near Neptune that may be solar system building blocks

This 3-D view of the solar system shows the orbit of the dwarf planet candidate 2026 ED138 in the location it held on May 8, 2026. It is among the largest and brightest objects discovered beyond Pluto, but had gone unnoticed until now.

NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA/R. Proctor

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The outer solar system is yielding its secrets to the Vera C. Rubin Observatory.

Less than five months into the observatory’s decade-long survey of the sky, a potential new dwarf planet has already popped up in its data, astronomers reported this week at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society’s Division of Planetary Sciences in Spokane, Wash.

Another team reported a handful of new Neptune Trojans, icy objects that share an orbit with Neptune, at the meeting and in the Astrophysical Journal Letters. The findings are filling in astronomers’ picture of the Kuiper Belt at the solar system’s frigid fringes.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“It feels a little bit like we’re replicating the 1800s and early 1900s, discovering what the solar system even looks like in general,” says Sam Deen, an amateur astronomer based in Simi Valley, Calif. “We’re finding out what there even is in the first place that makes up most of the Kuiper Belt.”

Perched on a mountaintop in Chile, the Vera Rubin Observatory is on a mission to map the entire southern sky every couple of nights, searching for faint and fast-moving cosmic objects. The observatory took its first images in June 2025 and officially began a decade-long survey in June 2026.

Even before the official survey started, Rubin had detected the motion of an object orbiting billions of kilometers beyond Pluto. Rubin observed the object 30 times on 20 nights from March 4 to July 11. But no one knew it was there until October 13, when astrophysicist Matt Holman of the Smithsonian Astronomical Observatory in Cambridge, Mass., ran a search for moving dots of light in the data.

The object, called 2026 ED138, appeared to be about 47 times as far from Earth as Earth is from the sun. Its brightness suggests it’s between 600 and 1,500 kilometers wide, potentially as large as other dwarf planets like Ceres and Makemake. That’s probably big enough to be spherical, making it a dwarf planet.

“It’s really big. It’s damn huge,” Deen says. “No matter what you call it, it’s still the biggest thing we’ve found in the entire solar system in 19 years.”

When Holman realized what he had found, he was thrilled but doubtful. “It’s quite an exciting thing,” Holman said in a news briefing at the meeting on October 27. “But one of the things that you need to do when you discover something potentially of this size is to try to verify that it’s true.”

Holman and colleagues were able to find observations of the same object in archived data from the Dark Energy Camera, located on an adjacent mountaintop in Chile, taken in 2016.

Deen was able to trace it back even farther, to photographic plates taken as part of a sky survey at Palomar Observatory in California in 1954. Other amateur astronomers independently found the same sightings.

“They took an image from Palomar in 1954, and another about half an hour after the first one, that both by pure chance happen to point at where ED138 is,” Deen says. “And it’s really obvious. If you know it’s supposed to be there, it’s not particularly faint.”

So why didn’t anybody notice it until now? It’s partly because ED138 practically crawls across the sky, orbiting the sun once every 280 years. It was also moving against a dense background of Milky Way stars, where it blended in.

By combining observations spanning decades, astronomers can calculate the object’s orbit with more precision.

Deen is hoping to observe the potential new dwarf planet pass in front of a distant star on Halloween. That sort of observation, called an occultation, can help reveal more details of the putative dwarf planet’s size and shape, and even whether it has moons or rings. Usually, it takes years to understand an object’s orbit well enough to predict an occultation, Deen says. “Getting to do it immediately is like being a kid in a candy shop, really.”

Caltech, Space Telescope Science Institute

Caltech, Space Telescope Science Institute

A crop of newly spotted Neptune Trojans were masked by the Milky Way, too. These asteroids gather in the same orbit as Neptune, but offset from the planet at 60 degrees. Astronomers think they were some of the original building blocks of the solar system and contain an ancient record of planetary formation and evolution.

Other planets have Trojans, too. Jupiter has thousands. Astronomers think Neptune has many more, but so far they have seen only 30 in the cluster of space objects that orbit ahead of Neptune, and just two in the cluster behind it.

“We would expect these [groups of Trojans] to be symmetric in numbers, so you have to get more than two,” planetary scientist Meg Schwamb said in a news conference at the meeting on October 28.

The trailing cloud happened to have been moving in front of the Milky Way from the perspective of Earth for the last 15 years. Spotting individual Trojans against that crowded background was “like finding a needle in a sequined dress,” said Schwamb, of Queens University Belfast in Northern Ireland.

Schwamb and colleagues examined Vera Rubin data taken from the commissioning phase — the period when engineers were testing the telescope. In this early data haul, the team found two more trailing Trojans, plus one candidate. They seem to be similar in composition to the leading ones, which matches theories of how the solar system formed.

“It just kind of got lucky,” Schwamb said. “These objects photobombed the commissioning survey.”

“This is really the appetizer for what Rubin Observatory is going to do in its mission for the next ten years,” she added. “There’s hundreds more of these objects likely to be found.”

Some of the excitement about these discoveries is dampened by fears of losing observations to bright satellites crisscrossing the telescope’s field of view, says astronomer Sam Lawler of the University of Regina in Canada.

“I have to put in the constant downer of how the increasing numbers of satellites will make these discoveries harder,” Lawler says. “There are one hundred new satellites launching every week, and they keep getting bigger and brighter. These discoveries will be hindered by that.”

But even with the satellites, Lawler anticipates many more cool discoveries from Rubin.

“Just finding a dwarf planet so quickly, maybe we’ll find something even bigger,” she says. “There could be something the size of Mars out there. And then we’d have the whole planet debate all over again. It would be fun.”

#6452. A farmer in Mexico saw the ground split open in his cornfield, then watched a volcano grow to 1,391 feet tall

In 1943, Mexico's Parícutin volcano erupted from a farmer's cornfield, growing rapidly and burying two villages during nine years of activity.

On February 20, 1943, farmer Dionisio Pulido watched a fissure open in his field near the village of Parícutin, in the Mexican state of Michoacán. Smoke rose from the crack, along with a hissing sound and a smell of sulfur.

Within a week, the new cone stood more than 490 feet (150 meters) tall. When the eruption ended in 1952, it had risen 1,391 feet (424 meters) above the cornfield where it began.

Lava buried two villages along the way. Parícutin was the first volcano whose eruption modern scientists observed in detail from its birth, according to the International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS).

Starting around February 5 to 7, 1943, local witnesses felt about two weeks of earthquake activity before the eruption.

Felipe Cuara Amezcua, then municipal president of San Juan Parangaricutiro, later reported that the tremors grew until more than 200 shook the area in a single day.

On February 20, Pulido went to his farm to prepare the fields for the spring sowing. He had owned the land for 31 years.

Smithsonian mineralogist William F. Foshag and Mexican geologist Jenaro González R. later collected his account and his wife’s. A 1956 U.S. Geological Survey bulletin printed them in English translation.

At about 4 p.m., Pulido left his wife, Paula, and went to burn a pile of branches. She had been hearing underground noise and thunder.

“About 4 p. m., after talking to my husband, I heard a kind of loud whistle,” Paula Pulido recalled.

“I saw that it was a kind of fissure that had only a depth of half a meter,” Pulido said.

He then saw the ground swell by about 6.6 to 8 feet (2 to 2.5 meters), while gray smoke or dust rose from the crack.

“Immediately more smoke began to rise, with a hiss or whistle, loud and continuous,” he recounted.

Frightened, he mounted his mare and galloped to the village where his family was waiting.

Accounts from Pulido and other witnesses gave “the first adequate account of the birth of a new volcano,” Foshag and González wrote.

One of the first photographs of the eruption, taken at 6 p.m. on February 20, shows an ash plume rising from the new vent. By midnight, the cone was about 20 feet (6 meters) high.

On the morning of February 21, a strong earthquake caused panic. People from Parícutin fled to San Juan Parangaricutiro, and many from San Juan went on to Angahuan or Uruapan.

A photograph from February 21 shows the cone about 100 feet (30 meters) tall, just rising above the treetops. After six days of activity, it reached 548 feet (167 meters).

The first lava flow, called the Quitzocho flow, moved north over cornfields prepared for planting. Mexican geologist Ezequiel Ordóñez estimated that the early lava advanced about 10 feet (3 meters) an hour.

Ash fell too. It piled up deeper than 6 inches (15 centimeters) over an area of 116 square miles (300 square kilometers) around the volcano.

When the first phase of activity ended on October 19, 1943, the original vent had built a cone about 1,200 feet (365 meters) high.

Pulido’s home village lay only 1.9 miles (3 kilometers) northwest of the new cone. Its 733 residents had to abandon it for good four months after the eruption began, and lava later flowed over the site.

Starting in January 1944, a new phase sent out the Taquí lava flows, which spread over about 7 square miles (18 square kilometers) by 1945.

In July 1944, lava surrounded the church of San Juan Parangaricutiro. Its tower still stands in the middle of a lava flow, the IUGS notes.

In all, the volcano’s lavas reached up to 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) from the vent and formed a field of about 9.7 square miles (25 square kilometers).

The Mexican government gave displaced residents new land in Caltzontzín, 17 miles (27 kilometers) to the southeast.

Parícutin was “the first well-documented example of an eruption of a monogenetic volcanic cone in historical time,” according to a 1993 USGS film report.

A monogenetic cone forms during a single eruptive episode. Parícutin, active for about nine years, gave scientists an unprecedented chance to follow such a volcano through its full life cycle.

An international group documented the activity in real time. Celedonio Gutiérrez, a resident of San Juan who kept a diary from the first day, worked with U.S. scientists throughout the eruption.

In 1990, volcanologists I. Yokoyama and S. de la Cruz-Reyna analyzed the precursory earthquakes of the 1943 eruption, a type of signal that comes before eruptions.

In 1985, decades after the eruption stopped, a fumarole at Parícutin still measured 883°F (473°C). The cone is one of more than 1,400 vents in the Michoacán-Guanajuato volcanic field.

The information was obtained from the Smithsonian Institution’s Global Volcanism Program.

An analysis of plant fossils preserved in amber from Myanmar revealed that the West Burma Block, a chunk of crust that broke off of Australia, seeded Southeast Asia's lush tropical forests.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Southeast Asia's tropical forests owe their rich biodiversity to a tiny fragment of Earth's crust that split from what is now northwestern Australia roughly 150 million years ago, a new study reports.

The fragment transported hundreds of flowering species and a flourishing collection of other ancient plants north across the prehistoric Tethys Ocean, the research reveals. The findings contradict previous theories that the fragment originated closer to what is now Southeast Asia and that Southeast Asia's tropical forests evolved sometime after the extinction of the dinosaurs around 66 million years ago.

At the time the fragment formed, Australia was connected to Antarctica and India within the ancient supercontinent Gondwana, which the Tethys Ocean separated from another ancient supercontinent, called Laurasia.

After drifting northward for 100 million years, the microplate eventually collided with Southeast Asia, seeding tropical forests that evolved into the lush ecosystems found in this part of the world today, the researchers said.

"The rich tropical rainforest flora of [Southeast Asia] is not endemic but owes much of its biota to the great southern land, Gondwana," study co-author Byron Lamont, a distinguished professor emeritus in Curtin University's School of Molecular and Life Sciences in Australia, told Live Science in an email.

But the collision with Southeast Asia was far from smooth, Lamont said. The fragment, which is known as the West Burma Block (WBB) or the Burma terrane due to its location in western Myanmar, wasn't the only piece of crust crossing the Tethys Ocean around 100 million years ago. The Indian subcontinent was also moving north, and it was doing so at a relatively rapid speed of 4 inches (10 centimeters) per year.

Around 80 million years ago, the Indian Plate bumped into the WBB, altering the fragment's orientation. The Indian Plate continued to shove the WBB until they both collided with Asia. The Indian Plate then slid beneath the Eurasian Plate to form the Himalayas, and the WBB ground to a halt to the west of present-day Myanmar, where it created a deep valley between mountain ranges about 35 million years ago, Lamont explained.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both the Indian Plate and the WBB "took some time to stop," he said.

From the time the WBB broke off from Gondwana until its collision with Southeast Asia starting 50 million years ago, the microplate spent tens of millions of years hovering near the equator, where it was humid and hot like it is today. This climate and the fragment's isolation provided a refuge where ancient plant lineages could survive and diversify, Lamont said.

For the study, Lamont and his colleagues examined more than 3,000 plant fossils from Myanmar that were preserved in amber around 100 million years ago. The fossils included flowers, leaves, fruits and seeds. They belonged to at least 392 types of flowering plants and a vast array of conifers, ferns, mosses, cycads and liverworts that reached Southeast Asia by floating on the WBB.

Amber has been mined from the north end of the WBB valley for at least a century, Lamont said. "Its beautiful fossils, preserved in 3D, have long attracted interest for their novelty value alone and there has been much commercial interest in them, especially from Chinese traders," he noted.

Some of the study's co-authors acquired chunks of amber from traders at least a decade ago, and they have been studying these pieces ever since. Advice was often required from experts at other institutions around the world, which is how Lamont got involved in the study, he said.

The findings, published Oct. 27 in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution, reveal the deep evolutionary roots of the tropical forests that grow in Southeast Asia today. The WBB didn't strip Australia of its ancient flora, because the descendants of many plants found in the 100 million-year-old amber still exist in the country's Northeast, which is hot and humid, Lamont said.

It's hard to say what kinds of animals arrived in Southeast Asia via the WBB, because only creatures small enough to be preserved in amber are represented in this fossil assemblage.

"The animals present in the amber are small insects, such as ants and mosquitoes," Lamont said. "Typical Australian vertebrates, such as marsupials, emus and nectar-feeding birds, arrived from South America in Australia over 100 million years later [after the WBB split off], and of course they would not have got caught in the resin even if they had been around."

#6449. Worker or queen? A genetic advantage may shape a fire ant’s future

A study of fire ants suggests a “selfish” supergene influences body size, potentially giving some ants a better chance of becoming queens.

Most red imported fire ants become workers. A few become queens, the largest ants in the colony and the ones that lay eggs.

How large an ant grows during development helps determine whether it becomes a worker or a queen.

A new study suggests that genes also influence this process.

In colonies with several queens, ants carrying a particular version of a large group of genes were more common among the biggest workers and future queens.

Haolin “Horace” Zeng and Brendan Hunt, insect researchers at the University of Georgia, studied this pattern in lab colonies.

Their work offers a clue to why these genes keep spreading, even though they can have drawbacks for the ants carrying them.

Some fire ant colonies have just one queen laying eggs, while others have many. A group of more than 500 genes helps determine which kind of colony develops.

These genes sit close together on a chromosome, a structure that carries DNA. They pass from parent to offspring together as a package called a supergene.

“We call them supergenes because the genes are tightly linked and inherited together, almost like one big gene,” explained Hunt, an associate professor in UGA’s entomology department.

The package comes in two versions. Scientists call the older version B and the newer one b, which appeared about one million years ago.

Ants in single-queen colonies have two copies of B, written as BB.

In invasive populations with several queens per colony, every egg-laying queen has one copy of each version, written as Bb.

Queens with the Bb combination weigh less and have more trouble starting colonies alone than BB queens. Yet the b version continues to spread.

Scientists describe it as a “selfish genetic element” because it improves its own chances of reaching the next generation, even when it does not help the ant carrying it.

Becoming a queen gives a female ant the opportunity to pass her genes to the next generation.

“If you want to pass down a gene, you’d better become a queen. You don’t want to become a worker,” Zeng said.

Young ants grow as larvae before becoming pupae, the stage when they change into adults. A natural chemical called juvenile hormone can delay the move out of the larval stage, giving them more time to eat and grow.

The researchers wanted to find out whether ants with the b version responded differently to this hormone.

In spring 2024, they collected colonies with one queen and colonies with several queens from Clarke and Oconee counties in Georgia.

They used these ants to set up small lab colonies without queens.

Each held about 2,500 workers, and all colonies received the same total weight of young ants at different developmental stages.

Some colonies received one meal containing methoprene, an artificial chemical that acts like juvenile hormone and is also used as an insecticide.

The others received a meal without it, and workers passed the food to the larvae.

Between 15 and 24 days after that meal, the team collected and weighed worker pupae. The middle weight, or median, was about three times higher in treated colonies than in untreated colonies.

The researchers then checked the genes of 1,049 worker pupae and 195 queen pupae from colonies with several queens. They compared the ants’ genes with their weight.

Ants carrying the b version became more common as body weight increased.

Here, ‘carrying the supergene’ refers specifically to the b version.

“Among the smallest workers, about half carried the supergene,” Hunt said. “That proportion increased to roughly 65% among the largest workers and 75% to 83% among queens.”

On average, BB pupae weighed about 19% less than Bb pupae. But the heaviest ants in each group weighed about the same, so the b version did not raise the upper limit on size.

Instead, ants carrying b reached the larger sizes more often.

The hormone treatment increased size by about the same amount in both groups, suggesting that a major difference in their response to this hormone did not explain the pattern.

The share of Bb ants also rose with weight at a similar rate among workers and queens.

That suggests the gene package affects body size, which then helps shape whether an ant becomes a queen, rather than having a separate effect on queen development.

“To me, it highlights that, through a developmental mechanism involving body size, a genetic element can alter caste outcomes and basically cheat its way into making a queen,” Hunt said.

The team next looked for genes that might explain the size difference. Scientists do not yet have a full record of which genes become more active as fire ant larvae grow into workers or queens.

The researchers therefore used existing data from pharaoh ants, which belong to the same ant subfamily.

Earlier work on adult fire ants had identified 191 genes that were more active in Bb ants than in BB ants.

Of those, 34 were also more active in pharaoh ant larvae developing into queens. That overlap was larger than the researchers would expect by chance.

One gene, called gas8, appeared in every comparison and sits within the fire ant supergene.

DNA near the start of gas8 is also more loosely packed in Bb fire ants, which fits with the gene being more active.

The team still does not know how the gene package changes growth.

Perhaps large BB larvae die more often before becoming pupae, or perhaps some Bb larvae spend longer eating and growing before moving to the next stage.

A computer simulation showed that extra growing time could produce the pattern seen in the study. Giving Bb larvae a better chance of continuing to a larger size could also explain it.

Workers might treat larvae carrying b more favorably, but that alone seems unlikely to explain the findings.

An earlier experiment found extra Bb queen pupae even when only BB workers raised them.

Researchers have not yet tested what gas8 does as ants develop. Experiments with fire ant larvae will be needed to find out.

Comparisons with other animals that carry supergenes could answer a wider question: do these gene packages often spread by changing how animals grow, or how long they spend growing?

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

#6447. Melting permafrost has birthed a new type of large landslide

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Wildfires and water underneath the ground could dislodge large chunks of frozen earth

In 2018, an immense landslide in Canada’s Mackenzie Valley dammed the Redstone River (shown) and created a 3.5-kilometer-long lake. Researchers say the event was a new type of large landslide called a permafrost detachment slide.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In 2018, a strange and enormous landslide occurred in Canada’s Northwest Territories. A slab of earth roughly equivalent in volume to seven Great Pyramids of Giza suddenly began sliding downhill, leaving behind a barren scar in the forested landscape. But what puzzled scientists was that the slide had initiated in frozen ground that had been glued in place for years.

An analysis of the event reveals that it represents a new class of catastrophic landslides called permafrost detachment slides, researchers report in the Sept. 28 Geophysical Research Letters. The slides may be set in motion by wildfires that occurred decades earlier, destabilizing the ground and opening cracks through which water infiltrated deep underground. Over time, that water may have thawed the frozen layer from below, eventually unleashing the entire frozen layer in a catastrophic slide.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Large landslides don’t normally mobilize so much still-frozen material, and when they do begin in thawing layers they usually move slowly, says Dmitry Nicolsky, a geophysicist studying permafrost at the University of Alaska Fairbanks who was not involved in the study. But he says this new research suggests scientists need to better study what’s occurring beneath the surface in permafrost regions, because “we don’t know how [the ground] will move — it might go slowly or it might go catastrophically.”

The inspiration for the research manifested in 2019, when permafrost geologist Joseph Young, based at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, Canada, at the time, was helicoptering to a field site in the Northwest Territories to assist a colleague’s research. In some of the valleys out there, the slopes were “just collapsing with landslides everywhere,” says Young, who is now at an engineering firm in Edmonton. That was surprising because they were in an area where the permafrost — ground that has been frozen for at least two consecutive years — shouldn’t have been thawing much.

Once on the ground, more puzzling details emerged. “Traditionally with permafrost, it melts from the top down, and that releases this slurry of muddy material,” Young says. But at some of the landslide sites, large blocks of still-frozen ground seemed to have been moved hundreds of meters, he says.

Young and his colleagues studied two of the largest slides in the region that had moved big chunks of permafrost. These were the 2018 slide, which mobilized 18 million cubic meters of earth and dammed the Redstone River, and another event in 2017 that moved 4.5 million cubic meters of material.

Field observations revealed that both events had initiated along flat sliding surfaces roughly 20 meters underground, where the permafrost layer’s base was identified. Meanwhile, satellite observations showed that the ground at both sites had been gradually moving meters each year for decades.

Young and his colleagues hypothesized that climate warming and wildfire had somehow played a role in causing the slides. They set up instruments nearby that tracked ground temperature from 2020 to 2022, focusing on spots either with undisturbed forest or where wildfire had burned about 25 years earlier.

They then plugged that data into computer simulations to estimate how the ground would have evolved in the decades after a fire. Based on the results, the researchers concluded that wildfire and extreme summer temperatures can warm and weaken the frozen ground surface, causing it to start creeping and form tension cracks. As these cracks grow, water can penetrate deeper into the frozen ground and eventually reach beneath the permafrost layer, causing it to thaw from below and eventually detach.

More than 150 other slides in the region, identified via satellite observations, may also have been permafrost detachment slides, Young says. This could occur wherever there’s a relatively thin and warm permafrost layer and a rapid warming event to set things in motion, he says.

Permafrost is thawing in cold regions around the world, and these huge slides are very visual manifestations of that, Young says. “This is a direct reality of a changing climate.”

#6446. Neanderthal heel bones reveal feet built for a demanding life

Neanderthals may have had flatter feet that helped them handle heavy loads and stay steady on rough ground.

A flatter foot may have helped Neanderthals support their heavy bodies and stay steady on rough ground.

A new study of fossil heel bones suggests that Neanderthal feet usually rolled inward and had a lower arch along the outside edge.

Researchers think this build may have suited the demands of their daily lives.

The study also found differences within our own species, Homo sapiens.

People who lived in Bologna, Italy, in the 19th and 20th centuries had slimmer heel bones than prehistoric hunter-gatherers, and their footwear and less active lives may help explain why.

Rita Sorrentino, now a professor at the University of Palermo, led the study, which University of Bologna professor Maria Giovanna Belcastro coordinated.

Belcastro said the analysis allowed the team “to highlight both an extraordinary biomechanical adaptation to withstand heavy loads and rough terrains, and the impact of modern life and footwear on our feet.”

No one can watch a Neanderthal walk, so the researchers looked for clues in the bones left behind. They used laser scans and CT scans to create 3D models of 71 adult heel bones.

Seven belonged to Neanderthals from sites in France, Spain, and Belgium. The youngest came from Spy Cave in Belgium and belonged to one of the last known Neanderthals in Europe.

The other 64 belonged to Homo sapiens. The oldest came from hunter-gatherers at Qafzeh and Skhul caves in Israel and dated to between 120,000 and 90,000 years ago.

The sample also included later Ice Age hunter-gatherers, Iron Age farmers from Sicily, and 46 people from a Bologna cemetery collection.

The researchers considered the Bologna group the least physically active population in the study.

The researchers marked 276 points along the edges and curved surfaces of each digital bone.

These points let them compare the heels in detail, while software estimated missing points on broken fossils from the parts that remained.

Neanderthal heels stood out in every comparison with Homo sapiens.

They were shorter from front to back, wider from side to side, and taller, although their overall size fell within the range seen in our species.

The biggest difference appeared at the back of the heel, where the Achilles tendon attaches. From behind, this area looked oval in Neanderthals and more triangular in Homo sapiens.

Neanderthals also had a much smaller bump underneath the heel, where a ligament that supports the arch attaches.

The researchers suggest this ligament may have provided less support, allowing the foot to bend more easily.

Belcastro linked the sturdy heels to the rest of the Neanderthal body.

“The robustness of the heel reflects the overall body structure of Neanderthals, which is characterized by a remarkable muscular and bone mass and an extremely intense level of physical activity,” Belcastro said.

“These physical characteristics indicate an adaptation aimed at promoting a greater load-bearing capacity on the back of the foot and a high mobility on uneven ground.”

The joints offered another clue. Where the heel meets the ankle bone, the joint surfaces were flatter and wider toward the outside of the foot.

That shape suggests Neanderthal feet normally rolled inward, a movement specialists call pronation.

Earlier research by Sorrentino’s group found signs of the same posture in Neanderthal ankle bones, on the other side of this joint.

In living people, rolling the foot inward brings more of those joint surfaces into contact and helps spread the load.

Neanderthals are thought to have carried more body mass than Homo sapiens, including more muscle, so this posture may have helped support their weight.

The researchers also propose that Neanderthals had a lower outer arch and a more flexible middle section of the foot.

Together, those features may have helped them stay steady as they crossed uneven ground.

An earlier study by the team found that a Neanderthal midfoot bone shared some features with those of adults diagnosed with flexible flatfoot. Most of those adults were overweight or obese.

Extra body weight may make feet roll inward and flatten their arches in people today. Still, similarities in bone shape do not prove that Neanderthal feet worked in exactly the same way.

Some differences may reflect ancestry rather than daily habits.

A small tunnel between the heel and ankle bones was shortest in Neanderthals, and its short length in other ancient human fossils suggests an inherited trait.

Within Homo sapiens, however, heel shape tended to vary with lifestyle.

In some ways, hunter-gatherers and even Iron Age farmers who also foraged had heels more like those of Neanderthals than those of the Bologna group.

Fossil footprints suggest that Neanderthals in Europe and later Ice Age Homo sapiens walked barefoot.

The Bologna group habitually wore heavy shoes and boots at work, and their heels differed from those of every earlier Homo sapiens group in the study.

Rigid footwear limits how far a foot can tilt from side to side.

The researchers suggest this restriction helped shape the joint at the front of the Bologna heels, which was taller and more curved.

The team also linked the Bologna group’s slimmer heels to footwear and a less active city life. But shoes alone cannot explain every difference.

“The morphology of our skeleton is not only the product of a strict genetic program, but also the consequence of physical stimuli and our daily life habits,” Belcastro said.

Ancestry, nutrition, and environment can also affect heel shape, the researchers wrote. The comparisons suggest that daily life matters, but they do not show how much each influence contributed.

The Neanderthal findings rest on just seven heels, several of which were damaged at the back and needed partial reconstruction.

The researchers also grouped men and women together because the samples did not allow them to test whether sex affected the results.

All the bones came from adults, leaving another question unanswered: how did Neanderthal heels develop that shape?

Their feet may have grown differently, responded to the strain of walking during childhood, or both.

A lower Neanderthal arch remains a hypothesis because bones alone cannot show exactly how a foot moved.

The researchers want future work to combine these shape comparisons with 3D models of foot motion to test the idea.

The study is published in the Journal of Human Evolution.

#6445. Methane emissions stayed stubbornly high despite a federal push to cut them

Satellite data show U.S. oil and gas methane emissions stayed nearly flat from 2019 to 2024, even as production grew and federal policies shifted.

Congress created the first federal methane fee in 2022 to encourage oil and gas companies to reduce emissions.

Satellite measurements now show that methane emissions from the sector remained near 11 million tons (10 million metric tons) a year from 2019 to 2024, with a slight increase in the final year.

The findings reveal no detectable decline following the law’s passage, though much of its enforcement framework had yet to take effect.

Methane emissions per unit of oil and gas produced fell by about 11% over the six years.

The researchers linked that decline mainly to new pipelines, better equipment, and earlier leak rules.

Ao Chen, a doctoral student at Johns Hopkins University, led the work with Scot Miller, an associate professor of environmental health and engineering there.

Colleagues at the University of Texas at Austin and McGill University took part.

Methane is nearly 30 times as potent as carbon dioxide at trapping heat, though it lasts a shorter time in the air. That makes it the second most important greenhouse gas to cut, Miller said.

Two instruments in orbit, Europe’s TROPOMI and Japan’s GOSAT, measure how much of it sits in the air below them.

The team fed roughly 2,000 of those readings a day over the lower 48 states into a model of how wind moves gas around. Then they ran it backward to work out where the methane came from.

The result is a map of emissions in boxes about 35 miles (55 kilometers) on a side, one for every day from 2019 to 2024.

Deciding how much of each box’s methane came from oil and gas rather than cattle or wetlands relies on existing inventories.

The team’s eight model runs show that choice can shift the oil and gas total by up to 20%.

The satellite totals ran about 17% above the EPA’s own inventory from 2019 to 2022. Earlier aerial and satellite studies have found the same gap, and some found it far wider.

Oil and gas methane across the lower 48 stayed between 10.3 million and 11.5 million tons (9.3 to 10.4 million metric tons) every year of the study.

It fell by about 640,000 tons (580,000 metric tons) from 2019 to 2023, then rose by about 230,000 tons (210,000 metric tons) in 2024.

Production, meanwhile, grew 8.5% over the same six years, so the methane released per barrel of oil and gas fell by 11.1%, or about 2.2% a year.

Most of that drop came between 2020 and 2022, before any new federal rule took hold.

“The good news is that emissions have not markedly increased, as many scientists feared would happen after an enormous increase in natural gas production in the decades following the hydraulic fracturing boom,” he said.

“The bad news is that oil and gas production is still a large percentage of U.S. methane emissions, and we do not find any evidence that a flurry of federal legislation had an impact on emissions.”

The Inflation Reduction Act created the Waste Emissions Charge, a fee on methane from large oil and gas facilities that was to begin in 2024.

It also set aside $1.36 billion to help companies find and fix leaks. The EPA finalized its own methane rules for new and existing wells in 2024.

Much of that framework had yet to take effect during the study.

The fee’s details stayed unsettled, and the rules for existing facilities gave states until 2026 to file their plans. Then Congress voided the fee rule in early 2025.

The EPA had projected the two measures together would cut 2024 emissions by about 420,000 tons (380,000 metric tons). The satellites saw an increase instead.

“We don’t see a detectable decrease in emissions after the Inflation Reduction Act,” Chen said.

“Of course, there’s no way to test the counterfactual. It’s possible that without the Inflation Reduction Act, methane emissions would be much higher.”

The biggest drop came from the biggest emitter.

Texas oil and gas methane fell 14%, from about 3.9 million tons (3.5 million metric tons) in 2019 to 3.3 million tons (3.0 million metric tons) in 2024. The state has no climate target.

The Gulf Coast Express line opened in late 2019, and the Whistler and Matterhorn Express lines followed, carrying gas from the Permian Basin to the coast and to Houston.

Pipeline access can allow producers to sell gas that might otherwise be flared or vented. Rising exports of liquefied natural gas made that gas worth more.

States with climate targets, among them California, Colorado, and New Mexico, cut oil and gas methane at rates that overlapped with states that have none.

Their inventories were more accurate, though. The satellite estimate was 3.6 times Texas’s official count and 5.8 times Oklahoma’s, while New Mexico’s matched.

California has pledged to cut its total methane 40% below 2013 levels by 2030.

That means cutting roughly 560,000 tons (510,000 metric tons) in four years, against about 130,000 tons (120,000 metric tons) over the past ten.

Colorado’s case is murkier. Its oil and gas methane swings by more than 30% from one year to the next, wider than the 26% cut its 2025 target demands.

That variability makes progress toward the target difficult to assess.

The study cannot establish what emissions would have been without the federal measures.

Continued satellite monitoring will help researchers track whether future policies and industry changes produce sustained reductions.

The full study was published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment.

A half-built neutrino telescope on the floor of the Mediterranean Sea searched for cracks in one of physics' most basic invariances. It came up empty, but its limits rival those of detectors many times its size.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The view from inside a detector building block, with the yellow buoy of a nearby detection unit clearly visible.

A particle-detecting telescope sunk more than a mile beneath the sea off the coast of France has tested a core principle of Einstein's relativity and found no cracks.

The detector, called Oscillation Research with Cosmics in the Abyss (ORCA), detects elusive particles called neutrinos. As a doctoral student, Alba Domi rode onto the Mediterranean aboard one of two boats that helped build the telescope, lowering some of its first detection units to the seafloor about 1.5 miles (2.4 kilometers) below the waves off Toulon, France.

Now, data from those first detection units have been used to test one of the founding rules of Einstein’s relativity: the idea that the laws of nature look the same no matter which way you face or how fast you move.

The team found no sign that this rule, called Lorentz invariance, is broken. But even with a detector only a fraction of its planned size, they set limits that compete with those of far larger and longer-running experiments.

The results were published Wednesday (Nov. 4) in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics.

Physics rests on two successful theories: general relativity, conceived by Albert Einstein more than 100 years ago, and the Standard Model of subatomic physics.

"General relativity describes the universe well on a cosmic scale, and the Standard Model of particle physics describes the microscopic scale; really, the single particles, how they behave," said study co-author Lukas Hennig, a doctoral student in advanced physics at Erlangen-Nürnberg.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both theories assume Lorentz invariance to be true. But in extreme settings, such as the first moments after the Big Bang, the two theories don't mesh. That has fueled a decades-long hunt for a theory of quantum gravity that unites them. Some candidates, including versions of string theory and loop quantum gravity, suggest that space-time might have a hidden "grain" at the tiniest scales — and that Lorentz invariance, "one of the most basic assumptions we make about our universe, might be violated," Hennig said.

Any such violation would be extremely small. To spot it, physicists would need a probe that could travel long distances and barely interact with anything along the way. Enter the neutrino.

Neutrinos are nearly massless particles that pass through Earth every second and carry zero charge. They barely interact with anything and come in three types: electron, muon and tau neutrinos. As neutrinos travel, they morph from one type into another in a predictable pattern that physicists call neutrino oscillation.

An optical module attached to the Dyneema ropes of the detection unit.

If Lorentz invariance were broken, that oscillation would change, with the effect growing more pronounced the farther the neutrinos traveled. So the team focused on neutrinos created when cosmic rays slam into the atmosphere elsewhere on the globe before traveling up through the planet to the detector. Some of the tested neutrinos crossed the entire 7,900-mile (12,700 km) width of Earth.

ORCA is part of the KM3NeT neutrino telescope. Each of its detection units is anchored to the seabed and holds 18 glass spheres packed with 31 light sensors apiece. When a neutrino collides with a particle in the water, it produces a faint flash of blue light that the sensors catch. The many sensors in each sphere help the team pin down which direction the light came from, Domi said.

Earth itself serves as a filter. The researchers selected only particles traveling upward through the planet, and they were able to weed out the flood of other particles from the atmosphere that would otherwise swamp the signal. "Only the neutrinos can get through," Hennig said.

That setup differs from that of IceCube, the Nobel Prize-winning detector buried in Antarctic ice. "Ice scatters the light more than water, but on the other hand, water absorbs the light more than ice," Domi said, which changes how each team reconstructs a neutrino's energy and path.

The researchers used 5,828 neutrinos collected over about 17 months between 2020 and 2021. They found that the oscillations matched standard physics. That means if Lorentz violation exists, it must be weaker than the limits the team set.

Those limits matter for theorists. If a model "predicts a Lorentz invariance violation [stronger than the new limits], the data rule it out. In that case, you can be pretty sure that this model is not correct," Hennig said.

The team also set the first direct limits on a kind of violation that would treat muon neutrinos and tau neutrinos differently.

The detector's limits on several key measures are competitive with those from Japan's Super-Kamiokande, which used 12 years of data, and from IceCube, which used two years of data from its full array.

"I'm surprised that we have competitive results with only six detection units," Hennig said. Today, 44 units are in the water, and the collaboration plans to activate 108 by 2030.

The best tests may still lie ahead. Because Lorentz-violating effects grow with distance and energy, neutrinos from distant cosmic sources are "actually the best candidates to do this kind of research," Domi said. The team plans to repeat the search using ORCA's sister detector, ARCA (Astroparticle Research with Cosmics in the Abyss), which sits off the coast of Sicily and is designed to catch those high-energy cosmic travelers.

If space-time does have a grain, those particles may be among the first to feel it.

Adriani et al. (2026). Atmospheric neutrino constraints on Lorentz invariance violation with the first six detection units of KM3NET/ORCA. Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics. https://doi.org/10.1088/1475-7516/2026/11/012
